# Labs

```{r setup-30, include=FALSE}
# include the helpers.R file for pdf output of youtube on pdfs as a clickable link
source("R/helpers.R")
# include the required packages to make sure the page can be built.
source("R/required_packages.R")
# jQuery is needed by kableExtra's kePrint.js (tooltips/popovers) but Quarto's
# Bootstrap 5 theme doesn't ship it by default.
inject_jquery()
```

This chapter is a **catalogue of labs**. It holds more labs than any one term can
deliver: an instructor picks the labs that suit their course, their own
background and the equipment available. Labs are identified by **name, not by
number** — no lab depends on where it sits in this chapter. Where labs *do*
depend on one another, the [catalogue](#sec-labs-catalogue) below and each lab's
*Prep work* say so.

The chapter is organised by **topic**. Each topic is a sub-chapter, and each lab
is a section within its topic. The last sub-chapter, [Teacher preparation](#sec-labs-teacher),
is a planning aid for the instructor: which labs must be delivered together, how
to schedule the materials-testing rotation, and the room, equipment, software and
shopping lists for every lab.

## How to use this chapter {#sec-labs-how-to .unnumbered}

Every lab is broken into the **same fixed parts**, and each part has its own
colour so you always know which part of the lab you are reading:

| Colour | Part | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| Dark blue | **Overview** | What the lab is about and why you do it |
| Teal | **Learning outcomes** | What you should be able to do afterwards |
| Orange | **Prep work** | Readings, videos and set-up to finish *before* the lab period |
| Blue | **Materials & equipment** | What to bring / what is provided |

::: {.callout-important}
## Where the step-by-step instructions live

The **detailed instructions, the tasks, the deliverables and the marking scheme
for each lab are delivered on FOL** as a **FOL quiz**
you complete *during the lab period*: it walks you through each task in order,
collects your written description of what you did, and is where you upload the
files you create (Rocksi stations, AnyLogic models, notebooks, model files,
screenshots and screen recordings). For the hands-on labs — metrology, quality
control, materials testing and virtual welding — the FOL quiz walks you through
each task, collects your measurements and answers, and is where you upload the
**lab worksheet or report template** you filled in. This chapter does not
reproduce the procedure or the rubric; open the FOL item for your lab and work
through it top to bottom.

**Unless a lab says otherwise, work is individual.** The labs that run in teams
(hands-on Gauge R&R and the materials-testing rotation) say so, and even there
**each student writes and submits their own report**.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Précitech Components — the running case

Many labs are set at **Précitech Components**, a Tier-1 automotive supplier in
Granby, Québec, whose CNC turning cells make transmission shaft blanks and whose
new shaft-kit assembly cell you design, simulate, balance, assess and finally
program a robot for (see the [case study](#sec-precitech-case) in the
*Engineering Design Process Documentation* lab). The metrology, quality-control,
materials and welding labs use lab hardware instead and are not tied to the
narrative.

**How the labs fit together:**

- **The Virtual Caliper precedes ML Week 2.** That is deliberately the arc
  Chapter @sec-chap-ml is built on: *do the SPC yourself first, then direct an
  LLM to do it.*
- **Facility Design & Simulation follows Engineering Design Process
  Documentation** — you turn your own layout drawing into a simulation.
- **Robotic Work-Cell Design checks its cycle time against the takt time you
  compute in the Lean lab.** It also bookends *Logic Thinking*: block-logic
  puzzles at the start of the course, a real industrial arm at the end.
- **TPM/OEE, Root Cause and a New Dataset follows the machine-learning set**
  because it reuses the whole ML pipeline on an unseen, differently shaped dataset
  — which only works once students have the skill.
- **The metrology labs underpin the quality-control labs** — a control chart or a
  Gauge R&R study is only as good as the measurement behind it.
:::

**Not in this catalogue:** the popsicle-stick bridge lab, the lean paper-cutting
simulation, and the automation/functional-safety lab series. The old handouts
still exist in the `LabInstructions/` folder and can be reinstated; the older
**instrumentation-trainer** stream (B1033 benches) is summarised in
[Appendix: instrumentation-trainer lab stream](#sec-labs-appendix-trainer).

Each lab is due at the end of its scheduled lab period; the late penalty is 25 %
per lab session. A take-home lab (Robotic Work-Cell Design) is released about
three weeks before its due date and includes a short screen recording. Marks may
be deducted for incomplete prelab work, missing safety training, not bringing
required materials or protective equipment, not cleaning your station, or
unprofessional conduct in the lab room. The course schedule in `index.qmd` shows
the plan the current offering follows; follow FOL if it diverges.

## Robotics and Programming Logic {#sec-labs-robotics}

Two labs that bookend a course: **block-based programming logic** on a
browser robot simulator, and the design and programming of a work cell for a
**real 6-axis industrial arm** in RoboDK. Neither needs an install. They pair with
Chapter 8 (Industrial Robotics).

### Logic Thinking for Robot Control: Rocksi {#sec-lab-logic}

::: {.lab-overview}
An introduction to programming logic — **sequencing**, **loops** and
**conditional/branching logic** — and to programming a robot arm, using one free
browser simulator: **Rocksi** (a browser, block-based simulator for a
collaborative robot arm — Scratch-style blocks, no install and no login). You
build the logic concepts *and* a pick-and-place sequence in the same tool, and
the focus is on *optimising* the number of blocks.

*(Earlier versions of this lab also used LightBot; it needs a Flash-era plug-in
that is not available on college machines, so the whole lab now runs in Rocksi.)*

**AI use:** not permitted — the outcome *is* your own logic. The [Robotic Work-Cell Design](#sec-lab-robodk) lab returns to a
real 6-axis arm in RoboDK for Web.
:::

#### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-outcomes}
After this lab you should be able to:

- Explain why programming logic matters for reliable, safe, repeatable automation.
- Use sequences, loops and conditional/branching blocks to solve a control
  problem with the fewest blocks.
- Describe the role of a teach pendant (jogging, teaching points, deadman/E-stop,
  reduced-speed teach mode, I/O testing).
- Program a simple pick-and-place-style sequence on a block-based robot simulator
  and simulate a digital input/output.
:::

#### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-prep}
- Read the [Programming Logic handout](labs/handouts/lab01-programming-logic.pdf)
  (importance of programming logic; loops; conditionals; teach pendants).
- Watch: *Rocksi robot simulator: Meet Sawyer*.

```{r video-rocksi, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
embed_youtube("3THTZFnrxtc", "Rocksi robot simulator: Meet Sawyer")
```

- Open [**Rocksi**](https://rocksi.net/) and confirm it loads and runs on your
  device. Try dragging one move block onto the workspace and pressing run.
:::

#### Materials & equipment {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-materials}
- Computer with internet access — **one per student** (all labs are individual)
- Access to [**Rocksi**](https://rocksi.net/) block-based robot-arm simulator
  (browser, free, no login, no plug-in)
- The **Snipping Tool** (Windows) for screenshots you will upload
- The **FOL quiz for this lab** — it carries every task, in order, and is where you type
  your answers and upload your Rocksi program and screenshots
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Instructions & submission"}
Work through the **FOL quiz for this lab** during the lab period. It covers sequencing,
loops, conditional/branching logic, a pick-and-place sequence, simulating a
digital I/O, and an optimisation challenge; for each task you describe what you
did and attach a screenshot, and at the end you upload your saved Rocksi program.
:::

### Robotic Work-Cell Design in RoboDK for Web {#sec-lab-robodk}

::: {.lab-overview}
A **take-home** lab: released about three weeks before it is due, done
individually, with a short screen recording as part of the submission. You design
and program the Précitech kitting cell's pick-and-place robot in **RoboDK for
Web** — a free, no-install, in-browser robot simulator with 600+ real arms. It
bookends [Logic Thinking](#sec-lab-logic): block-logic puzzles at the start, a real 6-axis
industrial arm at the end. You
close the loop on the course by checking the robot's cycle time against the
**takt time you computed in the [Lean](#sec-lab-lean-vsm) lab**.

**AI use:** permitted with disclosure. The station layout, the program and the
cycle times must be your own work.
:::

#### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-outcomes}
After this lab you should be able to:

- Jog a 6-axis robot in joint, linear and tool coordinates and recognise
  singularities and joint-limit stops.
- Lay out a work cell and verify that every pick and place point lies inside the
  robot's reach envelope.
- Program a pick-and-place cycle with targets and gripper I/O and read the
  simulated cycle time.
- Compare a simulated cycle time against a required takt time and optimise the
  program to close the gap.
- Compute a minimum safeguarding distance from robot stopping performance and
  select an appropriate safeguard.
:::

#### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-prep}
- Read Chapter 8 (industrial robotics — coordinate systems, the work envelope,
  singularities) and Chapter 6 (machine guarding — the minimum-distance /
  safeguarding-distance formula and the safeguard hierarchy).
- Have your **takt calculation from the Lean lab** to hand — you need the takt time for
  250 kits/day.
- Open [RoboDK for Web](https://web.robodk.com/simulation) and confirm it loads
  and runs a sample station in your browser. No account or licence key is
  required.
- Confirm your screen-recording tool works (the same tool the course plan's
  take-home lab uses).
:::

#### Materials & equipment {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-materials}
- Personal computer with internet access and a browser (this is a take-home lab —
  no lab PC required)
- [RoboDK for Web](https://web.robodk.com/simulation) — no install, no licence
  key
- A screen-recording tool — the built-in recorder is enough (Windows **Xbox Game
  Bar**, <kbd>Win</kbd>+<kbd>G</kbd>; macOS **Screenshot**,
  <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>5</kbd>) or free [OBS Studio](https://obsproject.com/)
- Your takt time from the Lean lab; the [Précitech case study](#sec-precitech-case) (250
  kits/day, one 8-hour shift)
- The **FOL quiz for this lab** — the five tasks in order, and where you upload the
  report, the RoboDK station file and the 3–5 min screen recording
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Instructions & submission"}
This is a **take-home** lab: released about three weeks before it is due, done
on your own computer. Work through the **FOL quiz for this lab** — it runs the five
tasks in order (jog and observe, build the kitting cell, program the
pick-and-place, cycle time vs the Lean-lab takt, and the safeguarding distance),
asks you to describe each design decision, and collects your report, the RoboDK
station file and a 3–5 minute screen recording talking through one decision. The
layout, the program and the cycle times must be your own work; disclose any AI
help.
:::

## Process Design and Simulation {#sec-labs-design}

The engineering documentation a new production cell needs before it is built, and
a discrete-event simulation of that cell — both set at Précitech Components. The
simulation lab builds on the documentation lab, so deliver them in that order.
They pair with Chapters 2, 4 and 16.

### Engineering Design Process Documentation {#sec-lab-design-doc}

::: {.lab-overview}
You produce the engineering-documentation package that a real project needs to
move a design into production — specification sheets, a bill of materials, a task
list / process flow, a project schedule and Gantt chart, a production-facility
layout drawing, and a health-safety-environment (HSE) risk assessment — for the
**Précitech Components shaft-kit assembly cell** described in the case study
below. The same cell is simulated in [Facility Design & Simulation](#sec-lab-anylogic), so the documents
you build here feed directly into the next lab. Tools: Microsoft Visio/Word,
Project and Excel.

**AI use:** not permitted for any part of the report.
:::

[]{#sec-precitech-case}

::: {.callout-note}
## Case study — Précitech Components: new shaft-kit assembly & packing cell

**Précitech Components** is a Tier-1 automotive supplier in Granby, Québec. Its CNC
turning cells produce transmission **shaft blanks** (AISI 4140 steel, Ø 25.000 mm
± 0.050 mm) for a major OEM customer. The OEM now wants the shafts delivered as a
**ready-to-install kit** rather than as loose blanks, so Précitech is adding a
**manual kitting, sub-assembly and packing cell** immediately downstream of the
CNC turning cells.

**One shaft kit contains:** 1 machined shaft blank, 2 tapered roller bearings, 1
retaining ring, 1 lip seal, 1 dowel pin, 1 desiccant sachet — placed in a moulded
tray inside a labelled carton. The exact part numbers, quantities and shaft
dimensions are on the assembly drawing
([410-2365, Rev B](labs/handouts/lab02-410-2365-shaft-kit-assembly-RevB.pdf)) and
shaft detail drawing
([205-5478, Rev B](labs/handouts/lab02-205-5478-shaft-RevB.pdf)) — you need both
for this lab.

**Target output:** 250 kits/day on one 8-hour shift.

**Process outline:** finished blanks arrive from the CNC cells on a trolley;
bought-in components (bearings, rings, seals, pins) are held in a small storage
rack that is replenished from the main warehouse when stock falls to a reorder
level; an operator picks the components for one kit, presses the two bearings onto
the shaft, fits the retaining ring and lip seal, inspects the assembly against a
checklist, places it in a tray, closes and labels the carton, and stages it for
the shipping dock.

Plant manager **Sophie Tran** has asked you to produce the engineering
documentation package for this cell **before it is built**.

*This is the same plant used in the machine-learning labs (see [Machine Learning](#sec-chap-ml-lab)), which build
a predictive-maintenance proof of concept for Précitech's CNC turning cells.*
:::

#### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-outcomes}
After this lab you should be able to:

- Explain terms such as HSE, Basic Engineering Design Data (BEDD), Front-End
  Engineering Design (FEED), fast-tracking, project schedule and General
  Arrangement (GA) drawing.
- Produce a specification sheet and a bill of materials for a manufactured product.
- Build a task list / process-flow chart with durations and turn it into a
  project schedule and Gantt chart in Microsoft Project.
- Draft a production-facility layout drawing showing product in/out, stations,
  storage, and material and people flow, and mark starvation / blockage risk
  points.
- Compare a highly automated (turntable) cell against a manual U-cell and
  justify a configuration choice for a given volume, timeline and labour
  situation.
- Complete an HSE risk assessment for a manual assembly cell.
:::

#### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-prep}
- Read the **case study** above and Unit 2 content on the basics of process
  engineering and design.
- Review the assembly drawing
  ([410-2365, Rev B](labs/handouts/lab02-410-2365-shaft-kit-assembly-RevB.pdf))
  and the shaft detail drawing
  ([205-5478, Rev B](labs/handouts/lab02-205-5478-shaft-RevB.pdf)) — you need
  the part numbers, quantities, materials and key dimensions from these for
  your spec sheet and BOM. Purchased components are sourced from
  **McMaster-Carr**.
- Skim the [Design Documentation supplement](labs/handouts/lab02-design-documentation-supplement.pdf)
  for the document templates and the detail-design / engineering process-flow
  diagram (ignore the popsicle-bridge framing — the document types are the same).
- Confirm you can open Microsoft Visio/Word, Project and Excel on a lab PC.
:::

#### Materials & equipment {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-materials}
- Lab PC with [**Microsoft Word**](https://www.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/word) /
  [**Visio**](https://www.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/visio/flowchart-software),
  [**Microsoft Project**](https://www.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/project/project-management-software),
  [**Microsoft Excel**](https://www.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/excel)
- Assembly drawing [410-2365, Rev B](labs/handouts/lab02-410-2365-shaft-kit-assembly-RevB.pdf)
  and shaft drawing [205-5478, Rev B](labs/handouts/lab02-205-5478-shaft-RevB.pdf)
  — the part numbers, quantities and dimensions you need
- Templates from FOL:
  - `Bill_of_Materials_Template_for_Excel.xlsx` — pre-filled with the kit's
    part numbers, descriptions and quantities from the assembly drawing; you
    fill in unit, source and supplier
  - `Gantt_chart_template.xlsx` — open it in Microsoft Project (File > Open)
    and use Project's Import Wizard to turn it into a schedule, then
    Save As `.mpp`; the template's "Read me first" sheet walks you through it
  - `Risk_Assessment_Template.docx` (HSE risk assessment)
- The Précitech shaft-kit case study (above) — the single source of requirements
- The **FOL quiz for this lab** — every phase in order, and where you upload your
  spec sheets, BOM `.xlsx`, flow chart, Project `.mpp`, layout drawing and risk
  assessment
:::

::: {.callout-note title="The automation decision"}

Précitech's plant manager has not committed to a cell configuration yet — that
choice is yours to make and defend as part of your facility layout. Two
realistic options are on the table for a 250-kit/day, single-shift cell:

**Option A — highly automated: rotary turntable, 6–7 stations.** An indexing
turntable carries the shaft through fixed stations (press bearing 1, press
bearing 2, fit retaining ring, fit seal, insert dowel pin + desiccant, inspect,
place in tray / close carton), with **one operator** at a single load/unload
station. Everything else is tooled and sensored.

**Option B — manual U-cell.** A standard U-shaped layout (Chapter 4) with **one
operator per station**, parts and trays moving between stations on roller
conveyors — matching the *manual* kitting cell Précitech originally scoped.

| | Option A — automated turntable | Option B — manual U-cell |
|---|---|---|
| Capital cost | High — custom turntable + tooled/sensored stations | Low — conveyor + hand tools/fixtures |
| Time to stand up | Long — design, build and debug before day 1 | Short — matches the "before it is built" schedule pressure |
| Labour | 1 operator/shift | Up to 6–7 operators/shift |
| Cycle-time consistency | High — paced by the index, not by people | Lower — depends on operator skill and fatigue |
| Flexibility to rebalance | Low — station count and index time are fixed | High — move people, cross-train, absorb absences |
| Changeover to a kit variant | Retool multiple stations at once | Operators adapt; fixtures swap faster |
| Failure mode | Single point of failure — one jammed station stops the whole cell | A blocked station can sometimes be buffered around |
| Ergonomic risk | Concentrated at one manual station | Spread across every station ([Ergonomics](#sec-lab-ergonomics)) |
| Maintenance skill needed | PLC/servo/automation technicians (Chapter 9) | Standard mechanical/tooling upkeep |

Neither option is "correct." Your facility-layout task in the FOL quiz asks you
to pick one, sketch it, and justify the choice with at least two pros and two
cons — from the table above or your own reasoning — tied to Précitech's actual
volume, timeline and labour situation.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Instructions & submission"}
Work through the **FOL quiz for this lab** during the lab period. It takes you through
all five phases — specification sheet and BOM (with a prepared checklist to work
from), task list / process flow, project schedule and Gantt chart, facility
layout drawing (including the automation decision above), and HSE risk
assessment — asks you to describe each one, and collects the electronic files.
The task-list and Gantt-chart examples in the quiz are **starting points only**
— part of the mark is finding and adding the steps they're missing. Keep your
layout drawing: you refine and reuse it in [Facility Design & Simulation](#sec-lab-anylogic). AI tools
may not be used for any part of this lab.
:::

### Manufacturing Facility Design & Simulation (AnyLogic) {#sec-lab-anylogic}

::: {.lab-overview}
You turn the Précitech kitting-cell layout from the [Engineering Design Process Documentation](#sec-lab-design-doc) lab into an electronic drawing,
then use **AnyLogic Personal Learning Edition** to run a discrete-event
simulation of the cell's order-fulfilment behaviour. By changing order and
replenishment parameters and reading the statistics screens, you see how
component-stock policy drives waiting time, picking (kitting) time and throughput.

**AI use:** not permitted for any part of the report.
:::

#### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-outcomes}
After this lab you should be able to:

- Produce an electronic facility layout showing stations, storage, flows, manual
  vs. automated stations, and starvation / blockage risk points.
- Run an AnyLogic model, change input parameters, and capture the statistics
  output.
- Interpret order statistics (preorder waiting time, picking time, full
  processing time, order states) and goods statistics (unavailable goods, stored
  reserved / unreserved goods, storing time) and explain how they are linked.
- Explain how simulation supports facility-design decisions such as where to hold
  buffer stock and how often to replenish.
:::

#### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-prep}
- Re-read the [Précitech case study](#sec-precitech-case) and review Unit 3
  content on integrated manufacturing systems.
- Read the [Facility Simulation supplement](labs/handouts/lab03-facility-simulation-supplement.pdf)
  (order statistics, goods statistics, and the relationships between them).
- Watch the AnyLogic walk-through video (link on FOL).
- Install [**AnyLogic Personal Learning Edition**](https://www.anylogic.com/downloads/)
  (free) on your machine *before* the lab and confirm it launches.
- Bring your layout drawing, spec sheets, schedule, BOM and flow documents.
:::

#### Materials & equipment {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-materials}
- Lab PC with [**AnyLogic Personal Learning Edition**](https://www.anylogic.com/downloads/)

## Lean Manufacturing {#sec-labs-lean}

Map, size and redesign a production flow. This lab pairs with Chapters 3 and 5,
and its takt time is used again in the robot work-cell lab.

### Lean: Value Stream Mapping, Takt and Pull {#sec-lab-lean-vsm}

::: {.lab-overview}
You map the Précitech shaft line as it runs today, size it against customer
demand, and redesign the flow. Working in **draw.io** (browser) you build a
current-state **value stream map**; in **Google Sheets** you compute **takt
time**, an operator balance chart and **process cycle efficiency**; and on
**AnyLogic Cloud** (browser, free public tier) you compare push, pull and a
kanban-capped supermarket. You finish with a future-state map carrying one SMED
and one pull improvement. Everything runs in a browser — nothing to install.

**AI use:** permitted with disclosure, but **not** for the map itself or the
takt / PCE calculations — those must be your own work. Name any tool you used and
what for.
:::

#### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-outcomes}
After this lab you should be able to:

- Draw a current-state value stream map from a station data table, with a
  material-flow line, an information-flow line and a lead-time ladder.
- Compute takt time from customer demand and compare it against station cycle
  times on an operator balance chart to find the bottleneck.
- Classify observed waste against the seven wastes and compute process cycle
  efficiency (value-added time ÷ lead time).
- Explain how push, pull and a kanban-capped supermarket differ in WIP and lead
  time, using simulation output as evidence.
- Propose a future state and justify the projected lead-time reduction.
:::

#### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted}

- Read Chapter 5 (Lean) on takt time, the seven wastes, pull systems, kanban and
  SMED, and the Chapter 3 material on line balancing.

  storage is fine, no account needed) and skim the built-in *Value Stream* shape
  library.
- Confirm [**AnyLogic Cloud**](https://cloud.anylogic.com/) loads and that you
  can run a public model and edit its input parameters in the browser.
- Download `vsm_station_data.csv` from FOL — the station table for the Précitech
  shaft line (cycle time, changeover, uptime, WIP, batch size per station).
:::

- Computer with internet access — one per student (all labs are individual)
- [**draw.io**](https://app.diagrams.net/) (browser) — current- and future-state maps
- [**Google Sheets**](https://sheets.google.com/) (browser) — takt, balance chart, PCE
- [**AnyLogic Cloud**](https://cloud.anylogic.com/) (browser, free public tier) — push/pull model
- `vsm_station_data.csv` from FOL

  8-hour shift
- The **FOL quiz for this lab** — the five tasks in order, and where you upload the
  draw.io exports, the Sheets calculations and the AnyLogic Cloud results

::: {.callout-note title="Instructions & submission"}
Work through the **FOL quiz for this lab** during the lab period. It runs the five tasks

## Metrology and Calibration {#sec-labs-metrology}

Dimensional measurement fundamentals: reading precision instruments, measuring
angles *indirectly* with gauge blocks and rollers, and calibrating an instrument
against a traceable standard. These hands-on labs sit underneath the SPC and MSA
chapters — a control chart or a Gauge R&R study is only as good as the
measurement behind it (Chapter 11). They are independent of each other and can
be delivered in any order; the instruments lab is the natural first one.

### Linear and Angular Measuring Instruments {#sec-lab-instruments}

::: {.lab-overview}
Before you can trust a measurement you have to understand the instrument that
made it. You study three linear instruments — the **vernier caliper**, the
**vernier height gauge** and the **vernier micrometer** — and one angular
reference, the **gauge (slip) block**. For each instrument you illustrate it,
label its parts, state the units of its scale(s), write the procedure for reading
it and derive the formula for its **least count**; you then work two least-count
problems and answer three questions on gauge-block grades, sets and wringing.

**AI use:** not permitted for the least-count calculations. Disclose any AI tool
you used for background research on the instruments.
:::

#### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-outcomes}
After this lab you should be able to:

- Identify the main parts of a vernier caliper, a vernier height gauge and a
  vernier micrometer, and state the unit of each scale.
- Read each instrument and explain, step by step, how the reading is built up
  from the main scale and the vernier or thimble scale.
- Calculate the least count of a vernier caliper and of a vernier micrometer
  from the way their scales are graduated.
- Explain what a gauge-block grade means, what each grade is used for, and how
  blocks are *wrung* together to build a stack.
:::

#### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-prep}
- Read the parts of Chapter 11 (MSA) on resolution, accuracy and calibration.
- Review how a vernier scale works: a sliding scale whose divisions are slightly
  shorter than the main-scale divisions, so the one line that aligns gives the
  fraction of a division.
- Bring a phone or camera — you photograph the instruments on your bench.
:::

#### Materials & equipment {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-materials}
- Vernier caliper, vernier height gauge and vernier (or digital) micrometer
- A gauge-block (slip-gauge) set — rectangular, square and square-with-hole
  blocks if the set has them
- The FOL quiz for this lab (and the lab assignment sheet on FOL)
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Instructions & submission"}
Complete the assignment sheet from FOL: one entry per instrument (illustration,
labelled parts, scale unit(s), reading procedure, least-count formula), the two
least-count problems, and the three gauge-block questions. Submit it in the FOL quiz.
The **FOL quiz for this lab** walks you through these steps in order and is where you record your results and upload your file.
:::

### Groove Angle Measurement (V-Block) {#sec-lab-v-groove}

::: {.lab-overview}
You measure the included angle of a V-groove *without* an angle-measuring
instrument. Two cylindrical rollers of different, precisely known diameters are
placed in the groove one at a time; with the V-block on a surface plate you
measure how high the top of each roller sits with a **vernier height gauge**. The
groove angle then follows from the two roller diameters and the two heights by
trigonometry. You repeat the whole procedure on four samples.

**AI use:** not permitted — the measurements and calculations must be your own.
:::

#### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-outcomes}
After this lab you should be able to:

- Explain the principle of measuring an angle indirectly from two roller
  diameters and two heights.
- Set up a vernier height gauge on a surface plate (zero at the plate, scriber
  just touching the roller) and read it.
- Calculate the V-groove angle from your measurements and comment on how well
  your repeats agree.
:::

#### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-prep}
- Review right-triangle trigonometry and inverse sine.
- Review how to zero and read a vernier height gauge (see
  [Linear and Angular Measuring Instruments](#sec-lab-instruments)).
- Read the precautions on the FOL sheet: the rollers must not move while the
  height is read, the scriber edge should only *just* touch the roller, and the
  roller diameter is measured at its middle.
:::

#### Materials & equipment {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-materials}
- V-block and a clean, dust-free surface plate
- Vernier height gauge and vernier caliper
- Two rollers (gauge pins) of different diameters
- The V-groove angle sheet from FOL (Table 1: roller diameter, roller height and
  calculated angle for each of four samples)
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Instructions & submission"}
Measure the two roller diameters with the caliper; place the smaller roller in
the groove and measure its height above the plate; repeat for the larger roller;
calculate the angle with the equation on the sheet and record it in Table 1; then
repeat the whole procedure for the remaining samples. Submit the completed table
in the FOL quiz.
The **FOL quiz for this lab** walks you through these steps in order and is where you record your results and upload your file.
:::

### Taper Angle Measurement with a Sine Bar {#sec-lab-sine-bar}

::: {.lab-overview}
A **sine bar** turns an angle measurement into a length measurement. The bar, a
stack of gauge blocks and the surface plate form a right-angled triangle: the bar
is the hypotenuse *L* and the gauge-block stack is the side *h* opposite the
angle, so $\sin\theta = h/L$. You build a gauge-block stack under one roller of
the sine bar until the top surface of an unknown **taper** is parallel to the
surface plate — confirmed by sliding a **dial indicator** along it and reading
zero deviation — and calculate the taper angle. You measure three tapers.

**AI use:** not permitted — the measurements and calculations must be your own.
:::

#### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-outcomes}
After this lab you should be able to:

- Explain the sine principle and why the two rollers must be equal in diameter,
  parallel, and a precisely known distance apart.
- Wring gauge blocks into a stack and use a dial indicator to prove that a
  surface is parallel to the plate.
- Calculate the half-angle $\theta = \sin^{-1}(h/L)$ and the whole taper angle
  $2\theta$, and compare it with the nominal taper angle.
:::

#### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-prep}
- Review right-triangle trigonometry.
- Review gauge-block wringing (see
  [Linear and Angular Measuring Instruments](#sec-lab-instruments)).
- Note that the dial-indicator reading tells you *which way* to adjust the stack:
  if the indicator deflects, add or remove gauge blocks and try again.
:::

#### Materials & equipment {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-materials}
- Surface plate, sine bar, dial indicator on a stand, gauge-block (slip-gauge)
  set
- Three tapers of different angles
- The sine-bar sheet from FOL (table: taper, gauge-block height *h*, bar length
  *L*, half-angle θ, whole angle 2θ, comparison with the actual taper angle)
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Instructions & submission"}
Follow the procedure on the FOL sheet for each assigned taper, record *h*, *L*,
θ and 2θ in the table, and compare with the actual taper angle. Submit the
completed sheet in the FOL quiz.
The **FOL quiz for this lab** walks you through these steps in order and is where you record your results and upload your file.
:::

### Micrometer and Caliper Calibration {#sec-lab-calibration}

::: {.lab-overview}
**Calibration** compares an instrument against a *traceable standard* — in
dimensional metrology, a gauge block whose deviation from nominal is known and
traceable to the international standard. You calibrate a micrometer and a
caliper: clean and inspect the instrument, let it come to ambient temperature,
set zero, then check it against gauge-block stacks at ten points spread over its
range, record the deviation at each point and report the instrument's accuracy
(the deviation over its range) against the manufacturer's published accuracy.
This is the first step of any measurement-systems analysis, and the reference
values it produces are what *bias* and *linearity* are measured against.

**AI use:** not permitted — the readings and the report must be your own.
:::

#### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-outcomes}
After this lab you should be able to:

- Explain calibration, traceability and why calibration is done at defined
  intervals.
- Carry out a calibration check on a micrometer and on a caliper following a
  standard procedure (clean, inspect, stabilise, zero, check at each size).
- Record and interpret the deviation at each size and decide whether the
  instrument is within its published accuracy.
- Complete a calibration report identifying the instrument, the standard used and
  the findings.
:::

#### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-prep}
- Read Chapter 11 (MSA) — calibration, bias and linearity.
- Review gauge-block wringing (see
  [Linear and Angular Measuring Instruments](#sec-lab-instruments)).
- Read the calibration procedure on the FOL sheet before the lab: the check sizes
  for the micrometer and for the caliper (which depend on its range) are listed
  there.
:::

#### Materials & equipment {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-materials}
- A micrometer and a caliper to calibrate (record make, model, serial number,
  range, resolution and published accuracy)
- A gauge-block set with its serial number, and clean lint-free wipes
- Cleaning fluid (methyl alcohol) — keep it off your skin
- The calibration report forms from FOL (one for the micrometer, one for the
  caliper)
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Instructions & submission"}
Complete one calibration report for the micrometer and one for the caliper:
instrument identification, the reading and deviation at each check size, the
accuracy over the range, the standard used, calibration notes and your
observations and findings. Submit both reports in the FOL quiz.
The **FOL quiz for this lab** walks you through these steps in order and is where you record your results and upload your file.
:::

## Statistical Quality Control and Measurement Systems {#sec-labs-sqc}

The laboratory companion to Chapter 10 (SPC) and Chapter 11 (MSA). Five of the
six labs are Excel worksheets: you collect real data — measuring roller bearings,
inspecting beads, measuring holes — and then do the statistics yourself in the
worksheet. The sixth, the Virtual Caliper, runs entirely on this page. Any lab
can be delivered on its own; a sensible order is *Statistics with Excel →
Variable Control Charts → Attribute Control Charts → Process Capability*, with
the two measurement-system labs (hands-on Gauge R&R and the Virtual Caliper)
alongside or after them. The *Virtual Caliper* and the hands-on *Gauge R&R* lab
cover overlapping ground — deliver one or both.

### Statistics with Excel for Quality Control {#sec-lab-excel-stats}

::: {.lab-overview}
Statistics is the language of quality control, and Excel is the tool most
quality technicians actually use. You learn the Excel functions for the basic
statistical parameters — average, median, mode, population and sample variance
and standard deviation, count, minimum, maximum and range — and apply them to
three small data sets: the processing times of 12 hot-rolled-steel samples
(compute the statistics and interpret the difference between mean, median and
mode), the depth of cut versus tool wear of a milling operation (20 observations,
plotted as a labelled scatterplot), and 50 call-centre waiting times (built into
a frequency table and a histogram, then read for the mean, the mode/median and
whether the shape looks like a normal curve).

**AI use:** not permitted — the calculations and graphs must be your own.
:::

#### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-outcomes}
After this lab you should be able to:

- Use Excel's statistical functions to compute measures of centre and spread, and
  explain when to use the population and the sample versions.
- Interpret the difference between mean, median and mode.
- Build a frequency table and histogram in Excel and judge whether a
  distribution looks normal.
- Plot and label a scatterplot to look for a relationship between two process
  variables.
:::

#### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-prep}
- Read the introductory sections of Chapter 10 (SPC) on variation, mean, standard
  deviation and histograms.
- Confirm you can use basic Excel formulas and insert a chart.
:::

#### Materials & equipment {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-materials}
- Computer with Microsoft Excel
- The statistics worksheet from FOL (the data sets, function list and answer cells
  are in the file)
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Instructions & submission"}
Work through the worksheet in order: the function warm-up, the processing-time
statistics with your interpretation, the scatterplot, and the histogram with the
four short-answer questions. Save the workbook and submit it in the FOL quiz.
The **FOL quiz for this lab** walks you through these steps in order and is where you record your results and upload your file.
:::

### Variable Control Charts: X̄, R and S {#sec-lab-variable-charts}

::: {.lab-overview}
You measure the length of **100 roller bearings** — in ten subgroups of ten — and
use the data to build an **X̄ chart**, an **R chart** and an **S chart** in Excel.
You compute the subgroup averages, ranges and standard deviations, the grand
average, the average range and average standard deviation, and the control
limits from the tabulated constants; then you plot the charts and evaluate them
against the out-of-control rules on the worksheet. (The bearings are tapered — you
measure length, *not* diameter.)

**AI use:** not permitted — the measurements, calculations and charts must be
your own.
:::

#### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-outcomes}
After this lab you should be able to:

- Organise measurements into rational subgroups and compute subgroup statistics.
- Calculate centre lines and control limits for X̄, R and S charts using the
  control-chart constants.
- Plot the charts and apply the out-of-control rules to decide whether the
  process is in statistical control.
- Explain the difference between what the X̄ chart and the R/S charts monitor.
:::

#### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-prep}
- Read Chapter 10 (SPC) — X̄/R and X̄/S charts, control limits and the
  out-of-control rules.
- Have the control-chart constants table to hand (the FOL sheet gives the
  constants for subgroups of ten; the full table is on FOL).
- Review how to read a micrometer or caliper to the resolution the sheet
  specifies.
:::

#### Materials & equipment {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-materials}
- 100 roller bearings (the same batch) and a micrometer or caliper
- Computer with Microsoft Excel
- The variable-control-charts worksheet from FOL and the control-chart constants
  table
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Instructions & submission"}
Measure the bearings in ten subgroups of ten and enter them in the worksheet,
complete the X̄, R and S calculations, plot the three charts, and evaluate the
charts against the out-of-control rules. Save the workbook and submit it in the FOL quiz.
The **FOL quiz for this lab** walks you through these steps in order and is where you record your results and upload your file.
:::

### Attribute Control Charts: p and np {#sec-lab-attribute-charts}

::: {.lab-overview}
Not every quality characteristic is a measurement — many are pass/fail. You
inspect a production run of coloured beads: in each of ten samples of 50 beads
you count the defectives (the instructor tells you which colour is "defective"
for your sample), then compute the proportion defective and build a **p chart**
and an **np chart** with their control limits. You judge whether the process is
in control and say what should be done next.

**AI use:** not permitted for the counts, calculations and charts. Your written
answers must be your own.
:::

#### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-outcomes}
After this lab you should be able to:

- Explain what a p chart and an np chart monitor and when to use each.
- Calculate the centre line and control limits for both charts (setting a
  negative lower limit to zero).
- Decide whether the process is in statistical control and justify the next step.
- Name a complementary tool (for example a Pareto chart) and say why it helps.
:::

#### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-prep}
- Read Chapter 10 (SPC) — attribute data, p and np charts.
- Review the difference between a *defect* and a *defective*.
:::

#### Materials & equipment {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-materials}
- A bag of beads of two or more colours per bench (enough for ten samples of 50)
- Computer with Microsoft Excel
- The attribute-charts worksheet from FOL
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Instructions & submission"}
Draw and inspect ten samples of 50 beads, record the number defective in each,
complete the p-chart and np-chart calculations, plot both charts and answer the
questions on the worksheet. Save the workbook and submit it in the FOL quiz.
The **FOL quiz for this lab** walks you through these steps in order and is where you record your results and upload your file.
:::

### Process Capability: Cp, Cpk and Distributions {#sec-lab-capability}

::: {.lab-overview}
A process can be in control and still not be **capable** — its natural spread
may be wider than the specification. You measure the length of **50 roller
bearings** with a micrometer, plot the data to see what distribution it follows,
compute the average, the average range and the standard deviation (both directly
and as the average range divided by $d_2$), and calculate **Cp** and **Cpk**
against the specification limits on the worksheet. A capable process has an
index of at least 1.33.

**AI use:** not permitted — the measurements and calculations must be your own.
:::

#### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-outcomes}
After this lab you should be able to:

- Plot a data set as a bar chart and scatter plot and describe its distribution.
- Estimate process standard deviation from the average range and from the raw
  data.
- Calculate Cp and Cpk and decide whether the process is capable.
- Explain why Cpk, not Cp, is the right index when the process is off-centre.
- Describe the steps of a real capability study — why the process must be stable
  and the parts must come straight from production.
:::

#### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-prep}
- Read Chapter 10 (SPC) — process capability, Cp and Cpk.
- Read the **Preparing a Capability Study** handout (FOL): the checklist a quality
  department follows before running a study — review history, size the sample,
  confirm the process is stable and the gauges are calibrated, quarantine and
  number the parts, and do not discard defective parts.
:::

#### Materials & equipment {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-materials}
- 50 roller bearings (the same batch) and a micrometer
- Computer with Microsoft Excel
- The capability worksheet from FOL, and the *Preparing a Capability Study*
  handout
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Instructions & submission"}
Measure the 50 bearings and enter them in the worksheet, plot the distribution,
compute the average, average range and standard deviation, then Cp and Cpk, and
state whether the process is capable. Save the workbook and submit it in the FOL quiz.
The **FOL quiz for this lab** walks you through these steps in order and is where you record your results and upload your file.
:::

### Repeatability and Reproducibility (Gauge R&R) {#sec-lab-grr}

::: {.lab-overview}
A measurement system has two sources of variation you can study directly:
**repeatability** (one person measuring the same item repeatedly) and
**reproducibility** (different people measuring the same item). In **Part A**, a
team of three operators each measures the diameter of five holes on a part with
a caliper, twice, and you work through the range-method calculation: the range
per hole and operator, the average ranges, repeatability, reproducibility, R&R,
part variation and total variation. In **Part B** you repeat the calculation on
a supplied two-operator data set. This is the hands-on, physical version of the
study you can also run in the browser in
[SPC and Gauge R&R: the Virtual Caliper](#sec-lab-spc-rr).

**AI use:** not permitted — the measurements and calculations must be your own.
:::

#### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-outcomes}
After this lab you should be able to:

- Explain repeatability and reproducibility and how each is estimated.
- Collect a balanced Gauge R&R data set (operators × parts × trials).
- Calculate repeatability, reproducibility, R&R, part variation and total
  variation with the range method, and express R&R against total variation.
- Judge whether a measurement system is adequate for the process it measures.
:::

#### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-prep}
- Read Chapter 11 (MSA) — repeatability, reproducibility and the range method.
- Review how to read a caliper to its resolution (see
  [Linear and Angular Measuring Instruments](#sec-lab-instruments)).
- Know your team: three operators (assigned by your instructor), each measuring
  independently.
:::

#### Materials & equipment {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-materials}
- A part with five measurable holes, and a caliper
- Computer with Microsoft Excel
- The Gauge R&R worksheet from FOL (Part A data sheet, Part B data set and the
  calculation steps)
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Instructions & submission"}
Part A: each operator measures the five holes twice and records the readings
independently; then complete the calculation steps in the worksheet. Part B:
complete the same steps on the supplied data. Save the workbook and submit it to
the FOL quiz.
The **FOL quiz for this lab** walks you through these steps in order and is where you record your results and upload your file.
:::

### SPC and Gauge R&R: the Virtual Caliper {#sec-lab-spc-rr}

::: {.lab-overview}
Before you ask an LLM to do statistical process control in Python (that is
[Machine Learning, Week 2](#sec-lab-ml-w2)), you do it yourself, by hand, as the measurement system. This lab runs
entirely inside this page: **webR cells** render a **virtual vernier caliper** at
a hidden, seeded true value, you read the scale and type the value, and the
readings you produce carry *genuine human reading error against known ground
truth* — so bias, linearity, repeatability and reproducibility are all
computable, which a paper Gauge R&R cannot do. You then build an X̄/R chart and
compute Cpk against the Précitech shaft spec of Ø 25.000 ± 0.050 mm.

**AI use:** not permitted for the readings or the calculations — *you* are the
measurement system being studied. You may use an LLM to check your written
reflection only, with disclosure.
:::

#### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-outcomes}
After this lab you should be able to:

- Read a vernier scale to its resolution and record a blinded, randomised
  measurement set.
- Run a range-method Gauge R&R: compute EV, AV, GRR, PV, TV, %GRR and the number
  of distinct categories (ndc), and judge gauge acceptability.
- Estimate gauge bias and linearity against certified reference values.
- Build an X̄/R control chart, apply the Western Electric rules, and compute Cpk
  against a two-sided specification.
- Explain how an inadequate measurement system distorts a capability index.
:::

#### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-prep}
- Read Chapter 10 (SPC — X̄/R charts, the Western Electric rules, Cpk) and
  Chapter 11 (MSA — bias, linearity, repeatability, reproducibility, the range
  method, ndc).
- Skim the worked webR cells in Chapter 11: `bias-calculation` and `range-method`
  — you reuse that method here.
- Nothing to install and no account to create. This lab needs **no external
  service** — if the book page loads, the lab works.
- You run the study **solo**: you play all three operator roles yourself, as
  three independent measurement rounds of the same 10 parts. Do the three rounds
  in separate sittings so each is a genuine re-read, not a copy of the last.
:::

#### Materials & equipment {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-materials}
- One computer with this book page open (a second screen helps — read the caliper
  on one, record on the other)
- The webR cells in this section (the caliper, the Gauge R&R calculator, the
  X̄/R + Cpk cell)
- A spreadsheet or paper grid to hold 90 readings (10 parts × 3 rounds ×
  3 trials) before you type them into the calculator cell
- The [Précitech case study](#sec-precitech-case): shaft blanks, AISI 4140,
  Ø 25.000 ± 0.050 mm
- The **FOL quiz for this lab** — the six tasks in order, and where you paste your
  reading grid and the cell outputs and upload screenshots of the X̄/R chart
:::

#### The lab cells {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.callout-note title="Instructions & submission"}
Work through the **FOL quiz for this lab** during the lab period. It runs the six tasks
in order — calibrate your eye, the 90-reading measurement run (three rounds of
10 parts × 3 trials), the range-method Gauge R&R, bias and linearity, the X̄/R
chart and Cpk, and the reflection — and asks you to paste your reading grid and
every cell output and to upload a screenshot of the X̄/R chart. The readings and
the calculations must be your own; you may use an LLM to check the written
reflection only, with disclosure.
:::

The quiz drives the webR cells below. They share one page environment and run
**top to bottom**: run the **setup cell first** and leave it run; every later
cell depends on the objects it creates. If a later cell errors with "object not
found", re-run the setup cell. Base R graphics only — do not add
`library(ggplot2)`; it is slow and fragile in webR and not needed here. Read the
virtual caliper to its **0.05 mm** resolution: the last main-scale mark the
vernier zero has passed, plus the vernier mark that best lines up with a
main-scale mark. When you play the three operator rounds, read blind — do not
look at your previous round's numbers.

```{webr-r}
#| label: caliper-setup
# ── Virtual caliper setup — RUN THIS FIRST ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# Defines the virtual caliper and the hidden true values. No third-party
# packages: base R graphics only.

set.seed(3027)

# Certified reference value of each of the 10 study parts (what a CMM reports),
# chosen to span the process range around the Ø 25.000 mm nominal.
caliper_ref <- round(sort(runif(10, 24.90, 25.10)), 3)

# The caliper under study has a small, slightly size-dependent bias (mm).
caliper_bias <- 0.03 + 0.05 * (caliper_ref - 25.00)

# What the caliper *shows* for a given part and trial: reference + gauge bias +
# a small amount of mechanism/technique slop. Seeded per (part, trial) so the
# same call always draws the same scene.
caliper_shown <- function(part, trial) {
  set.seed(1000L * part + trial)
  caliper_ref[part] + caliper_bias[part] + rnorm(1, 0, 0.015)
}

# Draw a zoomed vernier caliper (resolution 0.05 mm) at the shown value.
draw_caliper <- function(part, trial) {
  stopifnot(part >= 1, part <= 10, trial >= 1, trial <= 3)
  shown <- caliper_shown(part, trial)
  lo <- floor(shown) - 4
  hi <- lo + 24
  op <- par(mar = c(1, 1, 3, 1)); on.exit(par(op))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(lo, hi), ylim = c(3.5, 9), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
       main = sprintf("draw_caliper(part = %d, trial = %d)", part, trial))
  # fixed main scale (mm), ticks every 1 mm, labels every 5 mm
  for (m in lo:hi) {
    big <- (m %% 5 == 0)
    lines(c(m, m), c(7, if (big) 6.1 else 6.6), lwd = if (big) 2 else 1)
    if (big) text(m, 7.5, labels = m, cex = 0.9)
  }
  lines(c(lo, hi), c(7, 7), lwd = 2)
  text(lo, 8.6, "main scale — millimetres", pos = 4, cex = 0.9, font = 3)
  # sliding vernier: 20 divisions spanning 19 mm  ->  each 0.95 mm, resolution 0.05
  v0 <- shown
  for (k in 0:20) {
    xk <- v0 + k * 0.95
    big <- (k %% 5 == 0)
    lines(c(xk, xk), c(5.9, if (big) 5.0 else 5.5), lwd = if (big) 2 else 1)
    if (big) text(xk, 4.7, labels = sprintf("%.2f", k * 0.05), cex = 0.8)
  }
  lines(c(v0, v0 + 19), c(5.9, 5.9), lwd = 2)
  polygon(c(v0 - 0.22, v0 + 0.22, v0), c(6.0, 6.0, 6.5), col = "black")
  text(v0, 4.2, "vernier 0", cex = 0.8, font = 3)
  invisible(NULL)
}

# Randomised part order, one per operator (A, B, C).
operator_order <- lapply(1:3, function(i) { set.seed(70 + i); sample(1:10) })
names(operator_order) <- c("A", "B", "C")

cat("Setup complete.\n\n")
cat("Randomised part order:\n")
for (nm in names(operator_order))
  cat("  Operator", nm, ":", paste(operator_order[[nm]], collapse = " "), "\n")
cat("\nUse draw_caliper(part, trial) with part 1..10 and trial 1..3.\n")
```

```{webr-r}
#| label: caliper-demo
# Practice reads — set demo to 1, 2 or 3, run, write your reading, then check.
demo <- 1

practice_parts <- c(2, 6, 9)
p <- practice_parts[demo]
draw_caliper(part = p, trial = 1)
cat("Write your reading (mm) before running the next line.\n")
cat("Correct reading to 0.05 mm:",
    format(round(caliper_shown(p, 1) / 0.05) * 0.05, nsmall = 2), "mm\n")
```

```{webr-r}
#| label: caliper-grr
# ── Range-method Gauge R&R — 10 parts, 3 operator rounds, 3 trials ─────────────
# Replace the numbers below with YOUR 90 readings. Each round's matrix is
# 10 rows (parts 1..10) x 3 columns (trials 1..3). You produce all three rounds
# yourself (op_A = round 1, op_B = round 2, op_C = round 3).

op_A <- matrix(c(
#  trial1  trial2  trial3
   25.00,  25.05,  25.00,   # part 1
   24.95,  24.95,  25.00,   # part 2
   24.90,  24.95,  24.90,   # part 3
   25.10,  25.05,  25.10,   # part 4
   24.85,  24.90,  24.85,   # part 5
   25.20,  25.15,  25.20,   # part 6
   24.80,  24.85,  24.80,   # part 7
   25.15,  25.15,  25.10,   # part 8
   24.75,  24.80,  24.80,   # part 9
   25.25,  25.20,  25.25    # part 10
), ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)

op_B <- op_A + 0.01   # <-- replace with your round-2 readings
op_C <- op_A - 0.01   # <-- replace with your round-3 readings

trials    <- 3
operators <- 3
parts     <- 10

# AIAG average-and-range constants
K1 <- 0.5908                 # trials = 3   (repeatability)
K2 <- 0.5231                 # operators = 3 (reproducibility)
K3 <- 0.3146                 # parts = 10   (part variation)

ops <- list(A = op_A, B = op_B, C = op_C)

# Repeatability (EV): mean within-operator, within-part range
part_op_range <- sapply(ops, function(M) apply(M, 1, function(x) max(x) - min(x)))
Rbar <- mean(part_op_range)
EV   <- Rbar * K1

# Reproducibility (AV): range of the operator grand means, corrected for EV
op_means <- sapply(ops, mean)
Xdiff    <- max(op_means) - min(op_means)
AV       <- sqrt(max(0, (Xdiff * K2)^2 - (EV^2 / (parts * trials))))

# Gauge R&R
GRR <- sqrt(EV^2 + AV^2)

# Part variation (PV): range of the part averages across all operators & trials
part_means <- rowMeans(sapply(ops, function(M) rowMeans(M)))
Rp <- max(part_means) - min(part_means)
PV <- Rp * K3

TV   <- sqrt(GRR^2 + PV^2)
pGRR <- 100 * GRR / TV
ndc  <- floor(1.41 * PV / GRR)

cat(sprintf("EV  (repeatability)   = %.4f mm\n", EV))
cat(sprintf("AV  (reproducibility) = %.4f mm\n", AV))
cat(sprintf("GRR                   = %.4f mm\n", GRR))
cat(sprintf("PV  (part variation)  = %.4f mm\n", PV))
cat(sprintf("TV  (total variation) = %.4f mm\n", TV))
cat(sprintf("%%GRR                  = %.1f %%\n", pGRR))
cat(sprintf("ndc                   = %d\n", ndc))
cat("\nAIAG: %GRR < 10 acceptable | 10-30 marginal | > 30 unacceptable; ndc >= 5.\n")
```

```{webr-r}
#| label: caliper-bias
# ── Bias and linearity vs certified reference values ──────────────────────────
# Uses op_A / op_B / op_C from the caliper-grr cell and caliper_ref from the setup cell.

ops <- list(A = op_A, B = op_B, C = op_C)
obs_part_mean <- rowMeans(sapply(ops, function(M) rowMeans(M)))   # 10 part means
bias_by_part  <- obs_part_mean - caliper_ref

cat("Part | reference | observed mean | bias (mm)\n")
for (i in 1:10)
  cat(sprintf("%4d | %9.3f | %13.3f | %+7.3f\n",
              i, caliper_ref[i], obs_part_mean[i], bias_by_part[i]))

cat(sprintf("\nOverall bias = %+.4f mm\n", mean(bias_by_part)))

lin <- lm(bias_by_part ~ caliper_ref)
slope <- coef(lin)[2]
cat(sprintf("Linearity slope = %+.4f mm of bias per mm of size\n", slope))
cat(sprintf("Linearity over the %.2f mm study range = %.4f mm\n",
            diff(range(caliper_ref)), abs(slope) * diff(range(caliper_ref))))
```

```{webr-r}
#| label: caliper-spc
# ── X-bar / R chart and Cpk — seeded 25-subgroup production dataset ────────────
# Ø 25.000 +/- 0.050 mm. Same data for every group.

set.seed(250)
n_sub <- 25; n <- 5
USL <- 25.050; LSL <- 24.950; nominal <- 25.000

mu_series <- rep(25.002, n_sub)
mu_series[12:16] <- mu_series[12:16] + 0.030   # a real special-cause shift
x <- t(sapply(mu_series, function(m) rnorm(n, m, 0.011)))

xbar <- rowMeans(x)
R    <- apply(x, 1, function(v) max(v) - min(v))
xbarbar <- mean(xbar); Rbar <- mean(R)

A2 <- 0.577; D3 <- 0; D4 <- 2.114; d2 <- 2.326   # n = 5
UCL_x <- xbarbar + A2 * Rbar; LCL_x <- xbarbar - A2 * Rbar
UCL_R <- D4 * Rbar;           LCL_R <- D3 * Rbar

par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(xbar, type = "b", pch = 19, ylim = range(xbar, UCL_x, LCL_x),
     xlab = "Subgroup", ylab = "X-bar (mm)", main = "X-bar chart")
abline(h = c(UCL_x, xbarbar, LCL_x), lty = c(2, 1, 2), col = c("red", "black", "red"))
plot(R, type = "b", pch = 19, ylim = range(0, R, UCL_R),
     xlab = "Subgroup", ylab = "R (mm)", main = "R chart")
abline(h = c(UCL_R, Rbar, LCL_R), lty = c(2, 1, 2), col = c("red", "black", "red"))
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

sigma_hat <- Rbar / d2
Cp  <- (USL - LSL) / (6 * sigma_hat)
Cpk <- min(USL - xbarbar, xbarbar - LSL) / (3 * sigma_hat)

cat(sprintf("X-bar-bar = %.4f mm   R-bar = %.4f mm   sigma_hat = %.4f mm\n",
            xbarbar, Rbar, sigma_hat))
cat(sprintf("X-bar control limits: [%.4f, %.4f]\n", LCL_x, UCL_x))
cat(sprintf("Cp = %.2f   Cpk = %.2f   (automotive Tier-1 target: Cpk >= 1.33)\n", Cp, Cpk))
cat("\nBeyond-3-sigma subgroups:",
    paste(which(xbar > UCL_x | xbar < LCL_x), collapse = " "), "\n")
cat("Apply the remaining Western Electric rules by eye on the chart above.\n")
```

## Materials Testing {#sec-labs-materials}

Three destructive and hardness tests that show how a steel's heat treatment and
processing change its strength, hardness and toughness: **hardness testing**,
**tensile and microhardness testing of case-hardened steel**, and **Charpy impact
testing**. **These three labs run together as a rotation over three consecutive
weeks.** The class is split into three groups; each week every group is at a
different one of the three labs, and each group starts at a different lab, so by
the end of week three every student has completed all three (see
[Materials-testing rotation](#sec-materials-rotation)). Your instructor posts your group and your starting
lab on FOL.

::: {.callout-important}
## Safety in the materials laboratory

Wear **safety glasses and safety footwear** — you will not be admitted without
them. Do not handle dry ice with bare hands: use insulated gloves and tongs. Keep
alcohol off your skin (it is absorbed through it), keep etchant off your skin,
and stay clear of the pendulum's swing path in the Charpy lab.
:::

Testing is done in teams so that everyone can see the test, but **each student
writes and submits their own report** on the template provided on FOL.

### Hardness Testing: Rockwell and Brinell {#sec-lab-hardness}

::: {.lab-overview}
Hardness is a material's resistance to indentation, and it is the quickest test
of what a heat treatment has done to a steel. You measure the hardness of three
steel specimens — **annealed**, **quenched (hardened)** and **normalized** — with
two methods: the **Rockwell** tester (choosing the right scale, minor load and
major load) and the **Brinell** tester (measuring the indentation diameter and
converting it to a Brinell number). You average repeated readings, convert
between scales, calculate the percentage deviation and the reproducibility of
each method, and explain why the three heat treatments give different hardness.

**AI use:** not permitted for the readings and calculations. Your written answers
must be your own.
:::

#### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-outcomes}
After this lab you should be able to:

- Carry out Rockwell and Brinell hardness tests correctly, including scale and
  load selection.
- Convert between Rockwell and Brinell values using a conversion chart.
- Compare the reproducibility of the two methods for each specimen.
- Explain annealing, quenching and normalizing and relate each to the hardness
  you measured.
:::

#### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-prep}
- Read your notes on the heat treatment of steel — annealing, quenching and
  normalizing — and the difference between the Rockwell B and C scales.
- Review the definition of range (maximum minus minimum), which you use as your
  measure of reproducibility.
- Download the report template from FOL (*Hardness Testing*).
:::

#### Materials & equipment {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-materials}
- Rockwell hardness tester (with ball and diamond indenters) and Brinell hardness
  tester with a measuring microscope
- Annealed, quenched and normalized steel specimens
- Rockwell–Brinell conversion chart (or an online source)
- Safety glasses and safety footwear
- The hardness report template from FOL
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Instructions & submission"}
Test each specimen with both methods, record the readings in Tables 1 and 2 of
the template, complete the calculations, answer the questions and write the
conclusions on how closely the two methods agree and how reproducible each is.
Submit your own report in the FOL quiz.
The **FOL quiz for this lab** walks you through these steps in order and is where you record your results and upload your file.
:::

### Tensile and Microhardness Testing of Case-Hardened Steel {#sec-lab-tensile}

::: {.lab-overview}
A case-hardened part is hard on the outside and tough in the core. You examine
the microstructure of the **case** and the **core** of a case-hardened steel
(AISI 1566) and run a **Vickers microhardness traverse** from the surface inwards
in 0.5 mm steps, converting each indentation diameter to a Vickers and then a
Rockwell number. You plot hardness against depth and read off the **effective case
depth** (where hardness falls to HRC 50) and the **true case depth** (HRC 40). You
then test tensile specimens, plot their stress–strain curves and use them to
decide which material is the most brittle, the most ductile and the toughest, and
you calculate stress and strain for each.

**AI use:** not permitted for the readings, calculations and graphs. Your written
conclusions must be your own.
:::

#### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-outcomes}
After this lab you should be able to:

- Explain what case hardening does and how the microstructure of case and core
  differ.
- Perform a Vickers microhardness traverse, convert the results to Rockwell
  numbers and plot a hardness profile.
- Determine the effective and true case depths from the profile.
- Explain what a tensile test measures — yield strength, ultimate tensile
  strength, ductility — and calculate stress and strain from load and extension.
- Compare materials from their stress–strain curves: brittle versus ductile, and
  toughness as the area under the curve.
:::

#### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-prep}
- Read the **Tensile Testing and Microhardness Testing of Case-Hardened Material**
  slides from FOL — loading, stress, strain, the stress–strain curve, what the
  tensile test reveals, and how Vickers microhardness works.
- Review the formulas for engineering stress (load ÷ original area) and strain
  (extension ÷ original gauge length).
- Download the report template from FOL (*Tensile and MicroHardness Test*).
:::

#### Materials & equipment {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-materials}
- Case-hardened AISI 1566 specimen (mounted and polished) and a metallurgical
  microscope
- Vickers microhardness tester
- Tensile testing machine with data acquisition, and the tensile specimens
- Vickers-to-Rockwell conversion chart
- Safety glasses and safety footwear
- The tensile and microhardness report template from FOL
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Instructions & submission"}
Record the metallography sketches, complete the hardness table (depth,
indentation diameter, Vickers, Rockwell), plot the two hardness graphs, state the
effective and true case depths, then complete the tensile results and conclusions
in the template. Submit your own report in the FOL quiz.
The **FOL quiz for this lab** walks you through these steps in order and is where you record your results and upload your file.
:::

### Charpy Impact Testing and the Ductile-to-Brittle Transition {#sec-lab-charpy}

::: {.lab-overview}
Some steels are tough at room temperature and shatter when cold — the failure
mode behind brittle-fracture disasters in cold-weather structures. You break
notched **Charpy** bars of **AISI 1018 hot-rolled** and **cold-rolled** steel in a
pendulum impact tester at temperatures from well below freezing to above
boiling-water heat, recording the energy absorbed at each. Low temperatures come
from a bath of alcohol and **dry ice**; high temperatures from heated water. You
plot impact toughness against temperature for each steel, read off the
**ductile-to-brittle transition temperature (DBTT)**, and compare the fracture
surfaces (fine granular for brittle fracture, necking for ductile).

**AI use:** not permitted for the readings, calculations and graphs. Your written
conclusions must be your own.
:::

#### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-outcomes}
After this lab you should be able to:

- Explain what the Charpy value measures and how rate of loading, temperature and
  a notch affect toughness.
- Conduct Charpy tests safely at controlled temperatures, transferring the
  specimen and striking it within the time limit.
- Plot impact toughness against temperature and determine the DBTT for each
  steel.
- Describe and explain brittle and ductile fracture surfaces.
- Explain which crystal structure is susceptible to low-temperature brittleness
  and why the two steels differ.
:::

#### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-prep}
- Read the **Material Toughness, Charpy Impact Test, and the Ductile to Brittle
  Temperature Transition** slides from FOL — toughness, strain rate, notch
  effect, the Charpy test and the DBTT.
- Read the safety rules for the pendulum tester and for dry ice before the lab.
- Download the report template from FOL (*Charpy Impact Test*).
:::

#### Materials & equipment {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-materials}
- Charpy pendulum impact tester
- Notched AISI 1018 hot-rolled and cold-rolled Charpy specimens
- Temperature baths: alcohol and **dry ice** for the low temperatures (about
  −60, −40, −20 and 0 °C), room temperature, and heated water for the high
  temperatures (about 60 and 100 °C); a thermometer and tongs
- Insulated gloves, safety glasses and safety footwear
- The Charpy report template from FOL
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Instructions & submission"}
Hold each specimen at its test temperature for several minutes so the whole bar
is at temperature, and break it **within five seconds** of removing it from the
bath. Record the energy absorbed in the results table, plot impact toughness
against temperature for both steels, sketch or photograph the two fracture
surfaces, answer the questions, state the DBTT for each steel and write your
conclusions. Submit your own report in the FOL quiz.
The **FOL quiz for this lab** walks you through these steps in order and is where you record your results and upload your file.
:::
