## Virtual Welding {#sec-labs-welding}

Six progressive labs in **GMAW** (gas metal arc welding, often called MIG) on the
**Lincoln Electric VRTEX 360+** virtual-reality welding simulator. There is no
arc, no fume and no wasted metal: you practise on a simulated coupon while the
machine tracks your gun position, angle and travel speed and **scores every
weld**. The process is the one automated and robotic welding cells replicate, so
these labs give you the operator's view of what a welding cell has to get right.
In every lab you set the machine up **from a Welding Procedure Specification
(WPS)** — the document that fixes the shielding gas and flow rate, wire feed
speed, voltage and polarity for the joint — weld the coupon, and save your best
scored result. The labs share one routine (start-up, login, set-up screens,
monitor screens), so the first lab teaches it in detail and the later labs reuse
it. They build in difficulty in the order below, so it is best to deliver them in
that order, although any one can be delivered alone if students are given the
start-up routine first.

::: {.callout-important}
## Working on the simulator

- Log in with your username in the form **student ID + family name + first
  letter of your given name** (the first lab uses your first name). Every scored
  weld is saved under this name.
- Set-up values come **only from the WPS** for the joint you are welding. Wire
  feed speed and voltage have tolerances (for example ±5 in/min and ±1 V); a
  reading outside tolerance triggers an "Incorrect Settings" prompt.
- Practise as often as you like. **Save your best result to your flash drive and
  upload it in the FOL quiz.**
:::

### GMAW Flat Surfacing: Single Pass {#sec-lab-weld-flat-single}

::: {.lab-overview}
Your first lab on the simulator. You learn the machine — power-up, the coloured
function buttons, login, the set-up and monitor screens — then lay a **single-pass
stringer bead** on a flat 1/4 in mild-steel plate with GMAW short-circuit
transfer. The WPS supplies the settings: 75/25 argon–CO₂ shielding gas at
25–35 cfh, wire feed speed 250 in/min, 18 V, DC electrode positive (DCEP), with a
contact-tip-to-work distance of 3/8 in and a travel speed of 15 in/min.

**AI use:** not applicable — the work is hands-on in the simulator.
:::

#### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-outcomes}
After this lab you should be able to:

- Start up the VRTEX 360+, log in, and navigate the set-up and monitor screens.
- Read a WPS and set the shielding gas, flow rate, wire feed speed, voltage and
  polarity from it.
- Lay a single-pass stringer bead and interpret the score.
- Save your best result to a flash drive.
:::

#### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-prep}
- Read the **VRTEX 360 start-up** guide from FOL (power-up, login, gas and flow,
  wire feed speed and voltage, placing the coupon).
- Find this lab's WPS on FOL, or in the WPS booklet at the simulator using the
  index at the front (look up the identification number in the top right of the
  WPS).
- Bring a flash drive.
:::

#### Materials & equipment {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-materials}
- Lincoln VRTEX 360+ simulator
- The WPS for this weld (FOL or the WPS booklet at the simulator)
- The FOL quiz for this lab (and the lab assignment sheet on FOL)
- A USB flash drive
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Instructions & submission"}
Complete the lab assignment sheet — the start-up questions (the coloured buttons,
units, saving a weld, the monitor views) and the set-up values you took from the
WPS — then practise and save your best single-pass weld. Upload the saved weld to
the FOL quiz.
The **FOL quiz for this lab** walks you through these steps in order and is where you record your results and upload your file.
:::

### GMAW Flat Surfacing: Multi-Pass {#sec-lab-weld-flat-multi}

::: {.lab-overview}
You repeat the start-up routine and set the machine up from the WPS again, then
lay a **multi-pass** weld on the flat 1/4 in plate. Each pass has to be placed
relative to the one before it, so consistency of speed, work angle and
stick-out matters more than in a single pass.

**AI use:** not applicable — the work is hands-on in the simulator.
:::

#### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-outcomes}
After this lab you should be able to:

- Set up the simulator confidently from a WPS with minimal prompting.
- Lay overlapping multi-pass beads on a flat surface and compare the score of each
  pass.
- Identify from the monitor screens what you changed between passes and whether
  it improved the score.
:::

#### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-prep}
- Review the start-up routine and your notes and best score from
  [GMAW Flat Surfacing: Single Pass](#sec-lab-weld-flat-single).
- Find this lab's WPS on FOL or in the WPS booklet.
- Bring a flash drive.
:::

#### Materials & equipment {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-materials}
- Lincoln VRTEX 360+ simulator
- The WPS for this weld
- The FOL quiz for this lab (and the lab assignment sheet on FOL)
- A USB flash drive
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Instructions & submission"}
Complete the lab assignment sheet, then practise the multi-pass weld as many times
as you like and save your best result. Upload it in the FOL quiz.
The **FOL quiz for this lab** walks you through these steps in order and is where you record your results and upload your file.
:::

### GMAW Groove Weld: Single Pass {#sec-lab-weld-groove-single}

::: {.lab-overview}
You move from surfacing a plate to a **groove joint**: a butt joint in 3/8 in A36
plate, welded in the flat position (1G), with a backing strip, a 1/4 in root
opening and a 45° included groove angle. Unlike the surfacing labs, you change
the machine's default selection to match the WPS — 75/25 argon–CO₂, wire feed
speed 350 in/min, 20 V, DCEP — and you lay a single pass in the groove.

**AI use:** not applicable — the work is hands-on in the simulator.
:::

#### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-outcomes}
After this lab you should be able to:

- Select the weld type and joint on the simulator and set it up from the groove
  WPS.
- Explain how a groove joint differs from a surfacing weld.
- Complete a single-pass groove weld and interpret the score.
:::

#### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-prep}
- Review the start-up routine from
  [GMAW Flat Surfacing: Single Pass](#sec-lab-weld-flat-single).
- Read the groove-weld WPS (FOL or the WPS booklet): note the joint design, root
  opening and groove angle as well as the machine settings.
- Bring a flash drive.
:::

#### Materials & equipment {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-materials}
- Lincoln VRTEX 360+ simulator
- The groove-weld WPS
- The FOL quiz for this lab (and the lab assignment sheet on FOL)
- A USB flash drive
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Instructions & submission"}
Set up the machine from the WPS (the sheet asks for the gas and flow rate, wire
feed speed, voltage and polarity), practise the single-pass groove weld and save
your best result. Upload it in the FOL quiz.
The **FOL quiz for this lab** walks you through these steps in order and is where you record your results and upload your file.
:::

### GMAW Groove Weld: Multi-Pass {#sec-lab-weld-groove-multi}

::: {.lab-overview}
A thick joint cannot be filled in one pass. You weld the same groove joint with
a **multi-pass** sequence — the sheet has room to score up to **seven passes** —
and finish with a virtual **bend test**: if the weld is sound you earn a
**bend-test certificate**.

**AI use:** not applicable — the work is hands-on in the simulator.
:::

#### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-outcomes}
After this lab you should be able to:

- Plan and execute a multi-pass weld sequence in a groove joint.
- Record the score of each pass and see how the score changes as the joint fills.
- Explain what a bend test checks and what a pass or fail tells you about weld
  quality.
:::

#### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-prep}
- Review [GMAW Groove Weld: Single Pass](#sec-lab-weld-groove-single).
- Read the WPS for the multi-pass groove weld.
- Bring a flash drive.
:::

#### Materials & equipment {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-materials}
- Lincoln VRTEX 360+ simulator
- The groove-weld WPS
- The FOL quiz for this lab (and the lab assignment sheet on FOL)
- A USB flash drive
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Instructions & submission"}
Set up the machine from the WPS, weld and record the score for each pass, run the
bend test and note whether you earned the certificate. Save your best result and
upload it in the FOL quiz.
The **FOL quiz for this lab** walks you through these steps in order and is where you record your results and upload your file.
:::

### GMAW T and Lap Welds {#sec-lab-weld-t-lap}

::: {.lab-overview}
Fillet welds join two plates that overlap or meet at a right angle. In three
parts you weld a **T joint** in thin (10 gauge) sheet with a single pass, a **lap
joint** in 10 gauge with a single pass, and a **T joint in 1/4 in plate with three
passes**, all in the horizontal fillet position. Each part has its own WPS, so you
re-set the machine for each, and each finishes with a bend test.

**AI use:** not applicable — the work is hands-on in the simulator.
:::

#### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-outcomes}
After this lab you should be able to:

- Distinguish T, lap and groove joints and the weld each calls for.
- Switch the machine between joints and thicknesses by working from the right WPS
  each time.
- Complete single-pass and multi-pass fillet welds, score them and run the bend
  test.
:::

#### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-prep}
- Review the start-up routine and the multi-pass groove lab.
- Locate all three WPSs (T single-pass, lap single-pass, T multi-pass) before the
  lab.
- Bring a flash drive.
:::

#### Materials & equipment {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-materials}
- Lincoln VRTEX 360+ simulator
- The three WPSs for Parts A–C
- The FOL quiz for this lab (and the lab assignment sheet on FOL)
- A USB flash drive
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Instructions & submission"}
Complete Parts A, B and C on the assignment sheet — for each, the set-up values
from the WPS, the score of each pass and the bend-test result. Save your best
result of each weld and upload them in the FOL quiz.
The **FOL quiz for this lab** walks you through these steps in order and is where you record your results and upload your file.
:::

### GMAW Vertical T Welds {#sec-lab-weld-vertical-t}

::: {.lab-overview}
The hardest position on the simulator. You weld **T joints in the vertical
position** in two parts — a single pass in 10 gauge sheet, then a second T weld of
up to three passes — each set up from its own WPS. Working against gravity, you
must control the puddle with travel speed and gun angle much more carefully than
on a flat plate.

**AI use:** not applicable — the work is hands-on in the simulator.
:::

#### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-outcomes}
After this lab you should be able to:

- Explain why vertical welding is harder to control than flat welding.
- Set up and weld vertical T joints from the WPS and interpret the score.
- Complete the bend test and explain the result.
:::

#### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-prep}
- Review [GMAW T and Lap Welds](#sec-lab-weld-t-lap).
- Locate the vertical-T WPSs before the lab and note the direction of travel the
  WPS specifies.
- Bring a flash drive.
:::

#### Materials & equipment {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-materials}
- Lincoln VRTEX 360+ simulator
- The vertical-T WPSs
- The FOL quiz for this lab (and the lab assignment sheet on FOL)
- A USB flash drive
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Instructions & submission"}
Complete Parts A and B on the assignment sheet — the set-up values from each WPS,
the score of each pass and the bend-test result — then save your best result and
upload it in the FOL quiz.
The **FOL quiz for this lab** walks you through these steps in order and is where you record your results and upload your file.
:::

## Machine Learning: Predictive Maintenance {#sec-chap-ml-lab}

::: {.callout-important}
## Deliver as a set — do not cherry-pick

These six labs are **one six-week project**. Each week's output is the next
week's input, and the capstone rubric spans four of the six, so they are
delivered together, in order, or not at all.
:::

These six labs are the laboratory component of Chapter @sec-chap-ml. Each week
has two hours of classroom theory (Chapter @sec-chap-ml) followed by a two-hour
lab, and the six sessions build on each other: by the end of Week 5 you will
have a working predictive-maintenance web application at a public URL, and Week 6
is the live demo of it.

Each lab's tasks, deliverables and rubric are in that lab's **FOL quiz** (see
[How to use this chapter](#sec-labs-how-to)); the files you upload in the quiz are:

| Module week | Lab | Focus | Files you upload in the FOL quiz |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| 1 | [AI Literacy and Prompt Engineering](#sec-lab-ml-w1) | AI literacy: prompt engineering, hallucination hunting, Python code generation | `prompts.md` + `spc_starter.py` |
| 2 | [Manufacturing Data and SPC](#sec-lab-ml-w2) | Manufacturing data: cleaning, SPC, Cpk on real plant data | Completed `week2_lab.ipynb` |
| 3 | [The C-MAPSS Dataset](#sec-lab-ml-w3) | Capstone kickoff: understanding the C-MAPSS dataset | Notebook with sensor plots and reflection |
| 4 | [Building the Predictive-Maintenance Model](#sec-lab-ml-w4) | Capstone build: feature engineering, model training, evaluation | Notebook + `rul_model.pkl` + `feature_cols.pkl` |
| 5 | [Deploying the App](#sec-lab-ml-w5) | Capstone deploy: Streamlit app on the public internet | Public URL submitted via FOL |
| 6 | [Capstone Presentations](#sec-lab-ml-capstone) | Capstone presentations: live demo to the class | Presentation (no file submission) |

**Tools used across the module:**

- [**Google Colab**](https://colab.research.google.com) — free, no local installation required
- [**Claude.ai**](https://claude.ai) or [**ChatGPT**](https://chat.openai.com) (free tier) — for the Week 1–2 exercises
- [**GitHub**](https://github.com/) (free account) — required from Week 5; optional earlier
- [**Streamlit Community Cloud**](https://share.streamlit.io) (free) — required for the Week 5 deployment

**A note on using AI assistants in these labs:** you are explicitly encouraged to
use LLMs to help you write, debug, and understand code throughout this module.
However, you must be able to explain every line you submit. If the instructor asks
"why does this `groupby().transform()` reset the rolling window at each engine
boundary?" and you cannot answer, that line does not count as your work —
regardless of whether it runs correctly.

::: {.callout-note}
## The course narrative — Précitech Components

**You are a new process engineer at Précitech Components**, a Tier-1 automotive
supplier in Granby, Québec (the same plant documented in the [Engineering Design Process Documentation](#sec-lab-design-doc) and [Facility Design & Simulation](#sec-lab-anylogic) labs). The plant runs
CNC turning cells producing transmission shaft blanks for a major OEM customer;
your cell produces roughly 250 parts per day.

Your plant manager, **Sophie Tran**, has seen what GE and Toyota are doing with
predictive maintenance and wants to know whether Précitech can benefit too —
without leaking IP to public tools, without trusting unverified outputs, and
without a million-dollar infrastructure investment. She has assigned you to:

1. Learn enough about AI tools to use them safely and productively for daily
   engineering work (Weeks 1–2).
2. Build a proof-of-concept predictive-maintenance system using publicly
   available data and free tools (Weeks 3–5).
3. Present your findings and the deployed application to plant leadership (Week 6).

By the end of Week 5 you will have a working web application at a public URL. It
will not yet work on Précitech's actual machines — you used a NASA simulation
dataset, not plant data — but it will demonstrate the methodology, code quality
and user interface well enough for the plant manager to decide on next steps.
:::

### Machine Learning, Week 1: AI Literacy and Prompt Engineering {#sec-lab-ml-w1}

::: {.lab-overview}
The first lab of the machine-learning module. You compare
how an LLM responds to poorly vs. well-structured prompts, deliberately trigger
and document a hallucination, and use an LLM to generate the Python code you will
build on in [Machine Learning, Week 2](#sec-lab-ml-w2). Set in the Précitech narrative above.

**AI use:** required — you are assessed on directing an LLM well, not on writing
Python.
:::

#### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-outcomes}
- How an LLM responds to poorly structured vs. well-structured prompts.
- How to detect and document an LLM hallucination.
- How to generate Python code using an LLM and evaluate whether the output is
  trustworthy.
:::

#### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-prep}
- Read Chapter @sec-chap-ml, **Week 1** (the AI landscape; how LLMs work; why they
  fail; IP risk; the R-C-T-C-F prompt pattern).
- Create a free account on [Claude.ai](https://claude.ai) or
  [chat.openai.com](https://chat.openai.com) (free tier is fine).
- Create a text file `prompts.md` in your course folder — you add to it
  throughout the session and submit it at the end.
:::

#### Materials & equipment {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-materials}
- Computer with internet access — one per student (individual lab)
- An LLM chat account (Claude.ai or ChatGPT, free tier)
- `prompts.md` (you create it)
- No dataset or local install needed this week
- The **FOL quiz for this lab** — the four exercises in order, and where you paste your
  prompts and upload `prompts.md` and `spc_starter.py`
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Instructions & submission"}
Work through the **FOL quiz for this lab** during the lab period. It runs the four
exercises in order — bad prompt → good prompt with the R-C-T-C-F pattern, FMEA
summarisation at three audiences, the hallucination hunt, and LLM-assisted Python
starter code — asks you to paste each prompt and response and to say what changed,

able to explain every line of code you submit.
:::

### Machine Learning, Week 2: Manufacturing Data and SPC {#sec-lab-ml-w2}

::: {.lab-overview}
You run your Week 1 Python on real (messy) plant data — 90 days of production from

document each problem without silently deleting data, then build an X-bar control
chart and compute Cpk. This is the SPC you may have done by hand in the [Virtual Caliper](#sec-lab-spc-rr) lab, now directed
through an LLM.

## Maintenance and Root-Cause Analysis {#sec-labs-maintenance}

Bring OEE, the Six Big Losses, root-cause analysis and machine learning together
on one failing cell. It pairs with Chapters 12 and 15, and reuses the
[machine-learning](#sec-chap-ml-lab) pipeline, so it works best after that set.

### TPM/OEE, Root Cause and a New Dataset {#sec-lab-tpm-rca}

::: {.lab-overview}
You bring the whole term together on one problem: a Précitech CNC turning cell
that is not making its numbers. You compute **OEE** from a shift log and split the
losses into the **Six Big Losses**; you Pareto the failure modes; you run a
**5-Why and Ishikawa** root-cause analysis; and then you **direct an LLM** to
build a failure classifier on a *new* dataset — the **AI4I 2020 Predictive
Maintenance Dataset** from the UCI repository (CC BY 4.0, 10 000 rows, 5 labelled
failure modes). This is *classification* on a differently-shaped dataset, so the
C-MAPSS recipe from the capstone does not carry over — the point is to show you
can transfer the skill, not copy the code. Tools: **Google Sheets**,
**draw.io**, **Google Colab**.

**AI use:** required for the classifier task; permitted with disclosure
elsewhere. As in the ML module, you must be able to explain every line.
:::

#### Learning outcomes {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-outcomes}
After this lab you should be able to:

- Compute OEE (availability × performance × quality) from a shift log and
  attribute the losses to the Six Big Losses.
- Build a Pareto chart of failure modes and identify the vital few.
- Run a 5-Why and an Ishikawa (fishbone) analysis using measured process data as
  evidence.
- Direct an LLM to build and evaluate a classifier on an unfamiliar,
  class-imbalanced dataset, and choose metrics that survive the imbalance.
- Write the D4 (root cause) and D5 (corrective action) sections of an 8D report,
  tying model evidence back to the fishbone.
:::

#### Prep work {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-prep}
- Read Chapter 12 (TPM, OEE, the Six Big Losses) and Chapter 15 (troubleshooting,
  5-Why, Ishikawa, the 8D report).
- Skim your capstone notebook from the machine-learning module — you reuse the *workflow* (load,
  explore, split, train, evaluate) but not the code.
- Open the [AI4I 2020 dataset page](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/601/ai4i+2020+predictive+maintenance+dataset)
  and confirm you can download the CSV in the browser. Columns: air temperature,
  process temperature, rotational speed, torque, tool wear, a machine-failure
  flag, and five failure-mode flags — **TWF** (tool wear), **HDF** (heat
  dissipation), **PWF** (power), **OSF** (overstrain), **RNF** (random).
- Download `precitech_shift_log.csv` from FOL (one week of shift records for the
  CNC cell: planned time, downtime events, ideal cycle time, count, scrap).
:::

#### Materials & equipment {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.lab-materials}
- Computer with internet access
- [**Google Sheets**](https://sheets.google.com/) — OEE calculation and the Pareto chart
- [**draw.io**](https://app.diagrams.net/) — the Ishikawa diagram
- [**Google Colab**](https://colab.research.google.com) — the classifier
- `precitech_shift_log.csv` from FOL
- **AI4I 2020** CSV, downloaded in-browser from UCI
- Chapter 12 OEE definitions and Chapter 15 8D template
- The **FOL quiz for this lab** — the five tasks in order, and where you upload the
  Sheets OEE/Pareto file, the draw.io Ishikawa export and the Colab notebook link
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Instructions & submission"}
Work through the **FOL quiz for this lab** during the lab period. It runs the five
tasks in order — OEE and the Six Big Losses from the shift log, the failure-mode
Pareto on the AI4I data, the 5-Why and Ishikawa with measured feature evidence,
directing an LLM to build the failure classifier, and the 8D D4/D5 sections —
asks you to describe your method and results, and collects the Sheets file, the
draw.io export and the Colab notebook link. The classifier task requires an LLM;
disclose AI use elsewhere and be able to explain every line.
:::

## Teacher preparation {#sec-labs-teacher}

::: {.lab-shop}
Everything the instructor needs to prep the term: how to choose and schedule labs
from the catalogue (including the labs that must be delivered as a set), then the
room, equipment and software per lab, a consolidated shopping list, a
software/accounts checklist, and a room-booking checklist. Items marked
**[confirm]** are not stated in the source handouts.
:::

> The full term-prep material for the current offering — quickstart, term grid,
> grade-item checklist, paste-ready Course Plan notes, the AI-use policy, answer
> keys, rubrics and the per-lab failure modes for the labs it covers — lives in
> the **instructor handbook** (`instructor/instructor-guide.qmd`, renders to
> `instructor/instructor-guide.pdf` for FOL). The matrix below is the quick
> per-lab view.

### Choosing and scheduling labs {#sec-labs-scheduling}

This chapter holds more labs than one term can deliver, so **pick labs to fit your
course, your own background and your equipment.** Most labs stand alone. Three
groups of labs do not, and they are the constraints to plan around:

::: {.callout-important}
## Labs that must be delivered together

- **The machine-learning labs are a set — they cannot be cherry-picked.** The six
  labs form one six-week predictive-maintenance project: each week's output is the
  next week's input (`prompts.md` and `spc_starter.py`, then the cleaned SPC
  notebook, then the C-MAPSS notebook, then the trained model files, then the
  deployed app, then the presentation of that app), and the capstone rubric spans
  four of the six. Deliver all six, in order, in six consecutive weeks (each week
  pairs two hours of Chapter @sec-chap-ml theory with the two-hour lab) — or leave
  the module out.
- **The three materials labs are a 3-week rotation.** Deliver them over three
  consecutive weeks: split the class into three groups and have each group work
  through all three labs, each group starting at a different one — see
  [Materials-testing rotation](#sec-materials-rotation). All three labs run in the
  same room *every* week, so you cannot deliver just one or two of them.
  **The Charpy lab needs dry ice, and the lab technician needs two weeks' notice
  to order it for the three weeks.**
:::

**Dependencies between other labs** (deliver the first before the second):

| Lab | Needs first |
|---|---|
| Manufacturing Facility Design & Simulation (AnyLogic) | Engineering Design Process Documentation (its layout drawing becomes the simulation) |
| Robotic Work-Cell Design in RoboDK for Web | Lean: Value Stream Mapping, Takt and Pull (supplies the takt time) |
| Machine Learning, Week 2 | Machine Learning, Week 1 — and, ideally, the Virtual Caliper (the SPC done by hand) |
| TPM/OEE, Root Cause and a New Dataset | The machine-learning set (reuses the whole pipeline) |
| Any Virtual Welding lab after the first | GMAW Flat Surfacing: Single Pass (teaches the start-up routine) — *recommended*, not strictly required |

**Other planning notes**

- **Take-home lab.** Release Robotic Work-Cell Design about three weeks before it
  is due, and reserve 15 minutes in a lab period to demo the tool.
- **Statistical labs.** Deliver *Statistics with Excel* first if students are not
  yet comfortable with Excel; the Virtual Caliper and hands-on Gauge R&R overlap,
  so choose one or both.
- **Simulator and bench capacity.** Virtual welding and the bench labs are limited
  by the number of simulators and instruments; plan rotations accordingly
  **[confirm counts]**.
- The default plan for the current offering, lab by lab and week by week, is in
  the course schedule in `index.qmd`.

### Materials-testing rotation {#sec-materials-rotation}

Split the class into **three groups** (A, B, C). Each group starts at a different
lab and moves on every week, so all three stations run every week and every group
completes all three labs:

| | Week 1 | Week 2 | Week 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Group A** | Hardness Testing | Tensile and Microhardness | Charpy Impact |
| **Group B** | Tensile and Microhardness | Charpy Impact | Hardness Testing |
| **Group C** | Charpy Impact | Hardness Testing | Tensile and Microhardness |

- **Dry ice (Charpy lab).** One group is at the Charpy station each of the three
  weeks, so dry ice is needed in **all three weeks**. Give the lab technician the
  three lab dates and **at least two weeks' notice** to order it for the full
  three-week block; agree the quantity per session with them **[confirm]**. Dry
  ice sublimates, so it is normally collected on the day of the lab **[confirm
  with the technician]**.
- **Staff the Charpy station properly.** Cold-bath handling, dry ice and a swinging
  pendulum make it the highest-risk station; the technician or instructor should be
  at it for the whole period.
- **Each group needs its own specimens.** Count specimens per station per week (see
  the shopping list).
- Post the group list and the rotation on FOL before week 1 so students know which
  lab they start with and can do that lab's prep.
- Tests run in teams, but each student **submits an individual report** on the FOL
  template.

### Instructor notes by lab {#sec-labs-instructor-notes}

::: {.lab-shop}
Marking guidance and lab-specific prep, moved here from the individual lab
sub-chapters. For the software labs the tasks, deliverables and rubric each lab
is marked against live in that lab's **FOL quiz**; for the hands-on labs they are
on the FOL worksheet or report template. The full answer keys and per-lab failure
modes for the labs in the current offering are in the instructor handbook.
:::

#### Logic Thinking for Robot Control: Rocksi

::: {.lab-instructor}
- **Prep:** confirm [Rocksi](https://rocksi.net/) is reachable through the lab
  network/firewall *the day before* — it is the single point of failure for this
  lab. Have an offline fallback (screenshots / a slide walk-through) ready.
- **LightBot has been dropped:** it needs a Flash-era plug-in that is not
  available on college machines. The whole lab now runs in Rocksi — sequencing,
  loops, conditional/branching blocks, a pick-and-place sequence and a simulated
  I/O.
- Individual lab — one machine per student; no group submission.
- **Marking:** award the loop / conditional marks for the *explanation*, not just
  a working program. For the optimisation challenge, ask for the block count as
  evidence.
:::

#### Robotic Work-Cell Design in RoboDK for Web

::: {.lab-instructor}
- **Release three weeks before the due date** (in the default plan: week 11, alongside
  Week 5 of the machine-learning set, due at the end of week 14). This mirrors the course plan's existing
  take-home lab pattern (released three weeks out, video submission).
- **Prep:** the day before release, run through Tasks 1–3 in RoboDK for Web
  yourself on the college network — confirm `web.robodk.com` is reachable, the
  library loads, and a station can be saved and re-loaded. Have a reference
  station file and an expected cycle-time range (from the `R/make_lab_data.R`
  answer key) ready for marking.
- No lab room is needed — this is done from home — but reserve 15 minutes in a
  lab period to demo the tool and walk through the brief.
- **Marking:** the takt comparison in Task 4 only works if the student's takt from the
  Lean lab was correct; if it was not, mark Task 4 on the *method* against a takt you
  supply. Watch for cycle times that are physically implausible (joint speeds
  cranked past limits) — that is where the "your own work" line is tested.
:::

#### Engineering Design Process Documentation

::: {.lab-instructor}
- **Prep:** verify Microsoft **Project** and **Visio** licences are live on every
  lab PC (the parts most likely to be missing from a standard Office install).
  Run `python R/gen_lab_templates.py` to (re)generate the three FOL templates
  into `labs/templates/` and re-upload them each term; confirm the Gantt
  template's Import Wizard walk-through still matches your Project version, and
  save a native `.mpp` copy once you've verified it. Post the case study on FOL
  as its own one-page handout.
- **Continuity:** this lab and Facility Design & Simulation share the Précitech kitting cell. Tell
  students up front that the layout drawing they produce here becomes the model
  they build in the AnyLogic lab.
- **Marking:** look for traceability — the spec sheet, BOM, task list, schedule
  and layout should all describe the *same* cell and the *same* kit. Check the
  starvation / blockage annotations on the layout are present and sensible; they
  are the link to the AnyLogic lab.
:::

#### Manufacturing Facility Design & Simulation (AnyLogic)

::: {.lab-instructor}
- **Prep:** AnyLogic PLE install is the biggest failure point — push it to lab
  PCs ahead of the term and test a full model run. PLE has a model-size limit;
  confirm the demo model stays under it. Have the exact model file on FOL.
- Give the Phase 1 (facility-drawing) sign-off some rigour — students who skip it
  produce screenshots with no layout to tie them to. Check the layout matches
  their Design Documentation submission.
- **Marking:** the drawing carries ~40 % of the mark; analysis should reference
  the *specific* statistic that moved *and* the case-study consequence (e.g.
  "lower reorder level → more unavailable goods → longer preorder waiting time →
  kitting station idle, shipments late").
:::

#### Lean: Value Stream Mapping, Takt and Pull

::: {.lab-instructor}
- **Prep:** generate `vsm_station_data.csv` with `Rscript R/make_lab_data.R` and
  stage it on FOL. Publish the answer key from the same script — expected takt,
  bottleneck station, PCE and the push-vs-pull WIP/lead-time ordering.
- Build or fork the AnyLogic Cloud push/pull model once and confirm the input
  parameters students need (control policy, WIP cap) are exposed on the public
  run screen. Test it through the college firewall the day before.
- Confirm draw.io and cloud.anylogic.com are reachable on the lab network (see the software checklist below).
- **Marking:** the map and the takt/PCE arithmetic must be the student's own (AI
  not permitted for those). Check the lead-time ladder actually totals to the
  numbers quoted — a ladder that does not add up is the most common error.
- This is the takt reference for **Robotic Work-Cell Design** — students compare the RoboDK cycle
  time against the takt they compute here, so make sure the takt value is right.
:::

#### Ergonomics in Automated Manufacturing (REBA)

::: {.lab-instructor}
- **Print:** REBA worksheets + the REBA cheat sheet, one per student.
- Stage the three task video/photo sets on FOL (`Lifting Boxes.pdf`,
  `Workstation.pdf`, `Cleaning.pdf` and the matching clips).
- Individual lab — the FOL quiz assigns each student one of the three tasks;
  spread the assignments roughly evenly across the class.
- **Marking:** REBA scoring is where students lose marks — check the
  trunk/neck/leg and arm/wrist sub-scores and the coupling/activity adjustments,
  not just the final number.
:::

#### Linear and Angular Measuring Instruments

::: {.lab-instructor}
- **Prep:** post the assignment sheet; lay out one of each instrument per bench so
  students can photograph and label real instruments rather than copy pictures.
- **Post the corrected assignment sheet** (`Linear and Angular Measurements - fixed.docx` in `LabInstructions/Quality_Labs/fixed/`). The original caliper
  problem called the main scale's 1 mm division a "least count of 0.1 mm", which
  made the question ambiguous; both least-count problems are now worded
  unambiguously. **Answers:** caliper = 1 mm − 0.9 mm = **0.1 mm**; micrometer
  = 1 mm ÷ 50 = **0.02 mm** without the vernier and 0.02 mm ÷ 5 = **0.004 mm**
  with it.
- **Marking:** the derivation of the least-count formula, not just the number.
:::

#### Groove Angle Measurement (V-Block)

::: {.lab-instructor}
- **Prep:** confirm each roller pair is precisely measured and the roller
  diameters differ enough that both rollers touch only the sloping sides of the
  groove (as the sheet requires). Check the V-blocks and surface plates are clean.
- **Answer key:** the sheet's equation (a Word equation object) is
  $\alpha = 2\sin^{-1}\!\left[\dfrac{d_2-d_1}{2(h_2-h_1)-(d_2-d_1)}\right]$,
  with $d_1$, $d_2$ the roller diameters and $h_1$, $h_2$ the heights from the
  plate to the top of each roller.
- **Marking:** compare the repeats across the four samples; large scatter usually
  means the roller moved or the scriber pressed on it.
:::

#### Taper Angle Measurement with a Sine Bar

::: {.lab-instructor}
- **Prep:** confirm the length *L* of each sine bar (roller centre distance) and
  post it, and check the gauge-block set has fine enough steps to reach
  parallelism.
- Walk students through wringing once (see the Instruments lab).
- **Marking:** the sheet takes θ as the taper's *half*-angle and reports 2θ as the
  whole angle — check students follow that definition and compare 2θ with the
  tapers' stated angles.
:::

#### Micrometer and Caliper Calibration

::: {.lab-instructor}
- **Prep:** the source sheet's check sizes are **inch** sizes (micrometer 0.106 to
  0.954 in in nine steps; 6 in or 8 in caliper in ten steps of range/10). If your
  instruments are metric, substitute an equivalent sequence and update the report
  forms.
- The gauge-block set must carry a serial number and a certificate: the report
  asks for the standard's identification, and traceability is the point of the lab.
- Let instruments and blocks stabilise to room temperature before the lab starts;
  cold blocks from a cabinet give false deviations.
- **Marking:** the deviation at each size, the accuracy over the range compared
  with the published accuracy, and an actual finding (in / out of tolerance) rather
  than a restatement of the numbers.
:::

#### Statistics with Excel for Quality Control

::: {.lab-instructor}
- **Prep:** post the worksheet; check the students' Excel version supports
  `VAR.P`, `VAR.S`, `STDEV.P` and `STDEV.S`.
- **Marking:** the sheet carries its own mark allocations (interpretation of
  mean/median/mode, range/variance/standard deviation, the labelled scatterplot,
  the histogram and the four questions). Check the histogram bins match the ones
  given and that the "normal curve?" answer is argued from the shape.
:::

#### Variable Control Charts: X̄, R and S

::: {.lab-instructor}
- **Prep:** you need a batch of 100 roller bearings (or an equivalent part) and one
  measuring instrument per student or pair. The worksheet reads **length**; the
  bearings are tapered, so tell students *not* to measure diameter. Post the
  control-chart constants table (the constants for subgroups of ten are already in
  the sheet: A2 = 0.308, B3 = 0.284, B4 = 1.716, D3 = 0.223, D4 = 1.777).
- **Post the corrected worksheet** (`Variable Control Charts - fixed.xlsx`
  in `LabInstructions/Quality_Labs/fixed/`): its out-of-control rules now match
  the Western Electric rules in Chapter 10 (rules 1–4), plus two extra pattern
  rules (fifteen points within 1σ; eight points none within 1σ).
- **Marking:** the subgroup statistics, the limits, the three charts and a
  justified in/out-of-control call.
:::

#### Attribute Control Charts: p and np

::: {.lab-instructor}
- **Prep:** put together bead bags with a known mix of colours, and tell each
  student (or bench) a different "defective" colour so results cannot be copied.
- **Marking:** the p-chart limits use the sample size *n* = 50; a negative lower
  limit is set to 0. Check the reasoning on "what to do next" and on the
  complementary tool (a Pareto chart is the expected answer).
:::

#### Process Capability: Cp, Cpk and Distributions

::: {.lab-instructor}
- **Post the corrected worksheet** (`Process Capability - fixed.xlsx`
  in `LabInstructions/Quality_Labs/fixed/`). The original Cp formula lacked
  brackets (it now reads (USL − LSL) / (6σ)) and told students to use Cpk "if the
  distribution is not normal" — Cpk is the index for an **off-centre** process, and
  the corrected sheet says so.
- The specification on the sheet is USL = 0.5008 and LSL = 0.4992 (inches).
  Confirm it suits the bearings and micrometer you supply.
- **Marking:** the σ estimate two ways (R̄/d₂ and STDEV.P), Cp, Cpk, and the
  capable / not-capable decision against 1.33.
:::

#### Repeatability and Reproducibility (Gauge R&R)

::: {.lab-instructor}
- **Prep:** assign teams of three and give each team a part with five measurable
  holes; operators measure independently and must not see one another's readings.
- **Post the corrected worksheet** (`Repeatability and Reproducibility - fixed.xlsx` in `LabInstructions/Quality_Labs/fixed/`). The
  original used the 10-part constant (3.18) and an unexplained "÷ 40". The corrected
  sheet uses the 5.15σ convention with **d₂ = 1.128** (2 trials), **d₂\* = 1.91**
  for three operators (Part A) or **1.41** for two (Part B), **d₂\* = 2.48** for
  five parts, and **n × r = 10** (5 holes × 2 trials); it also adds a %R&R step.
  (The virtual-caliper lab uses 1σ-based constants; %R&R is a ratio and is
  unaffected by the convention.)
- **Part B answer key** (corrected constants): average ranges 6.44 and 6.46;
  EV ≈ 29.4; the reproducibility term is negative, so AV = 0; R&R ≈ 29.4;
  Vp ≈ 82.2; Vt ≈ 87.3; **%R&R ≈ 34 %** — unacceptable (over 30 %).
- **Marking:** the step-by-step calculation, R&R versus total variation, and a
  judgement on whether the gauge is adequate.
:::

#### SPC and Gauge R&R: the Virtual Caliper

::: {.lab-instructor}
- **Prep:** none beyond opening the rendered page and checking the webR cells
  load. This lab has **no external dependency** — no site, no account, no
  dataset file.
- Run `Rscript R/make_lab_data.R` to print the Virtual Caliper answer key: the
  `caliper_ref` values, the expected overall bias (≈ +0.03 mm), and the expected
  %GRR / ndc / Cpk ranges. The caliper and SPC data are generated inside the
  webR cells, so there is no file to stage.
- Individual lab — each student plays all three operator rounds themselves, in
  separate sittings. A reading grid where the three rounds are identical (or
  every trial matches) was not read blind.
- **Marking:** check that %GRR and ndc are consistent with the EV/AV/PV reported.
- This lab is the "do it yourself first" half of the arc into Machine Learning, Week 2 (SPC in
  Python, directed by an LLM). Point that forward explicitly.
:::

#### Hardness Testing: Rockwell and Brinell

::: {.lab-instructor}
- **Prep:** stage annealed, quenched and normalized specimens and check the two
  testers are calibrated with test blocks. Post the report template.
- Safety glasses and safety footwear are required; keep students clear of the
  indenter when loading.
- **Marking:** the average and % deviation, the reproducibility (max − min) for
  each method, and a reasoned explanation of why the hardened specimen gives a
  narrower spread than the annealed one. For the online-conversion questions,
  Rockwell C 51 and Brinell 500 are roughly equivalent, as are Rockwell B 85 and
  Brinell 165 — check against your conversion chart.
:::

#### Tensile and Microhardness Testing of Case-Hardened Steel

::: {.lab-instructor}
- **Prep:** mounted, polished case-hardened AISI 1566 specimens; 2% nital etchant
  and polishing consumables if students etch (keep alcohol and etchant off skin,
  ventilate); tensile specimens of **two or more** different materials so that the
  most-brittle / most-ductile / toughest comparison has something to compare.
- Tell students to bring a memory stick if the tensile machine's data are saved to
  file **[confirm]**.
- The template defines the effective case depth at HRC 50 and the true case depth
  at HRC 40 — check that matches the convention you teach.
- **Marking:** the hardness table and the two graphs, the case depths read from
  them, and stress and strain calculated with the working shown.
:::

#### Charpy Impact Testing and the Ductile-to-Brittle Transition

::: {.lab-instructor}
- **Order dry ice two weeks ahead** through the technician, for all three weeks of
  the rotation.
- **Prep:** notched AISI 1018 hot-rolled and cold-rolled specimens (the template
  has seven temperature rows: about −60, −40, −20, 0 °C, room temperature, 60 and
  100 °C). Set up the alcohol/dry-ice bath and the hot-water bath before the
  period so specimens can equilibrate for several minutes.
- **Safety:** insulated gloves for dry ice, never sealed in a container, keep the
  room ventilated. Before each swing, make sure everyone is clear on both sides of
  the pendulum and out of its striking distance; the specimen is centred on the
  anvil with the notch facing away from the striking edge. The break must be made
  **within five seconds** of leaving the bath.
- **Marking:** the plotted curves, a DBTT read from each curve, the fracture-surface
  descriptions (fine granular vs. necking), and the answers on the Charpy value
  and BCC crystal structure.
:::

#### Virtual Welding (all six labs)

::: {.lab-instructor}
- **Prep:** power up the VRTEX 360+ units before the lab (they need two or more
  minutes to start), check the WPS booklets are at the simulators, and post the
  start-up guide, the WPSs and the six assignment sheets on FOL. Students need a
  flash drive for their best weld.
- **The FOL quiz for each welding lab replaces the source PDF assignment sheets**,
  which are not editable and contain copy-paste slips (the quizzes carry the
  correct titles and steps): the flat-surfacing multi-pass sheet is titled "Single Pass"; the groove
  single-pass sheet is headed "Lab Assignment 2" and describes flat surfacing; the
  T-and-lap file is named for lab 4 but headed lab 5; the vertical-T sheet's Part B
  is headed "Lap Single Pass" but selects **T 10GA** and scores three passes. The
  single-pass and multi-pass groove labs cite the **same WPS**, whose table lists
  two passes while the multi-pass sheet has seven score lines. The WPS pages for
  the flat multi-pass and vertical-T welds were not among the supplied files —
  confirm they are in the booklet.
- **Marking:** compare the set-up values on the sheet with the WPS (within the
  stated tolerances), check the saved weld belongs to the student's login, and
  record the score and any bend-test result.
:::

#### Machine Learning, Week 1: AI Literacy and Prompt Engineering

::: {.lab-instructor}
- **Prep:** confirm Claude.ai / ChatGPT and colab.research.google.com are
  reachable on the lab network. Post the FMEA table (Chapter @sec-chap-ml, Week 1)
  and a blank `prompts.md` on FOL.
- No dataset needed this week; `spc_data.csv` is staged for Week 2.
- **Marking:** Exercise 3 is the point of the week — require genuine verification
  (a screenshot of the empty ASTM search, a Google Scholar "no results"), not
  just "I think this is made up".
- The capstone (Weeks 3–6) is assessed together against the capstone rubric held
  in FOL and the instructor handbook.
:::

#### Machine Learning, Week 2: Manufacturing Data and SPC

::: {.lab-instructor}
- **Prep:** stage `spc_data.csv` and `week2_lab.ipynb` on FOL. Keep a key of the
  embedded problems (row indices, correct fixes) for marking.
- The most common error is using the standard deviation of the daily means for
  the control limits instead of `sigma_individual / sqrt(n)` — check this
  explicitly.
- Follow up on a `spc_starter.py` line from Week 1: ask a student to explain it.
- **Marking:** deduct for silent row deletion even if the final chart looks
  right — the traceable quality log is the learning objective.
:::

#### Machine Learning, Week 3: The C-MAPSS Dataset

::: {.lab-instructor}
- **Prep:** stage `train_FD001.txt` and `predictive_maintenance.ipynb` on FOL
  (host the dataset yourself so it does not depend on Kaggle sign-in during the
  lab). Confirm Colab is reachable.
- The "sawtooth" reflection question (Task 5.1) sets up the engine-wise split in
  Week 4 — make sure students actually answer it.
- **Marking:** rolled into the capstone rubric; here just verify the notebook
  runs end to end and the reflection is attempted.
:::

#### Machine Learning, Week 4: Building the Model

::: {.lab-instructor}
- **Prep:** none beyond Week 3 — same notebook, same data. Have a reference
  solution notebook with the expected RMSE (~21 cycles) and feature-importance
  chart.
- **The teaching moment:** circulate during the evaluation task and look for RMSE
  < 10 — that is the row-wise-split data leak. Make students diagnose it
  themselves via the split assert.
- **Marking:** rolled into the capstone rubric.
:::

#### Machine Learning, Week 5: Deploying the App

::: {.lab-instructor}
- **Prep:** stage `streamlit_app.py` and a known-good `requirements.txt` on FOL.
  Walk through one full deploy yourself the week before — Streamlit Cloud and
  GitHub UIs change. Confirm github.com and streamlit.io are reachable on the lab
  network.
- Have students do the GitHub / Streamlit account creation as prep, not in the
  lab — it eats 20 min otherwise.
- **If you are delivering the take-home Robotic Work-Cell Design lab, release it this week** (three weeks before it is due).
- **Marking:** rolled into the capstone rubric; the deliverable is a URL that
  loads and predicts.
:::

#### Machine Learning, Week 6: Capstone Presentations

::: {.lab-instructor}
- **Prep:** build the presentation schedule; test the projector with a couple of
  student URLs beforehand; have your own reference app ready to show if a
  student's deployment is down.
- **Stretch goals** continue in [TPM/OEE, Root Cause and a New Dataset](#sec-lab-tpm-rca), which reuses this
  pipeline on the AI4I 2020 dataset: XGBoost comparison, SHAP values, FD002
  generalisation, prediction intervals.
- The Weeks 3–6 capstone rubric (100 points: working model 30, code quality 20,
  Streamlit app 25, documentation & honesty 15, presentation 10) and its
  weighting are maintained in FOL and the instructor handbook; publish them
  before the module starts.
:::

#### TPM/OEE, Root Cause and a New Dataset

::: {.lab-instructor}
- **Prep:** generate `precitech_shift_log.csv` with `Rscript R/make_lab_data.R`
  and stage it on FOL; publish the expected OEE and Pareto order from the answer
  key the script prints. Host a copy of the AI4I 2020 CSV on FOL as a fallback in
  case UCI is unreachable from the lab.
- Confirm `archive.ics.uci.edu`, draw.io and Colab are reachable on the lab
  network the day before.
- Individual lab.
- **Marking:** Task 4 is the point of the lab. A student who reports high
  accuracy and stops has missed it — full marks require *noticing* the imbalance
  and switching to precision/recall (or a resampling / class-weight fix). Reused
  C-MAPSS code that does not fit tabular data is a red flag that the transfer did
  not happen.
:::

### Consolidated shopping list (buy / restock each term)

Tick only the labs you are delivering. The software-only labs (Rocksi, RoboDK,
AnyLogic, Lean, ML, TPM) use **no physical consumables**; the bridge and
lean-simulation labs that did are not in the catalogue. If either is reinstated
from `LabInstructions/`, restore its shopping list from the previous revision of
this chapter (git history) or the original handouts.

### Appendix: instrumentation-trainer lab stream {#sec-labs-appendix-trainer}

An older set of labs for this course code was written for the **B1033** trainer
benches (author "MZhang"). They are **not** part of the current lab set, but the
handouts are in the `LabInstructions/` folder and are summarised here in case the
course runs them:

| Alt lab | Title | Room | Equipment | Software |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| Alt — Pressure/level | Pressure Measurement for Level | B1033 | Trainer: power-supply module, pump/tank unit, RTD temperature transmitter, pressure transmitter, float/reed switch, 2 × DMM, banana leads | — |
| Alt — Motor control | Motor Control & Intro to VFDs | B1033 | 3-phase motor, FVNR (full-voltage non-reversing) starters, control-relay/MCR wiring, E-stop, pilot lights, pushbuttons; VFD | — |
| Alt — PLC | PLC Introduction with Siemens | B1033 | Siemens PLC trainer, field devices (pushbuttons, selector switches, pilot lights, cylinders with proxy sensors), potentiometer 0–10 VDC, DMM | **Siemens TIA Portal**; reference video `YOvQhvjaeqY` |
| Alt — Flow rate | Flow Rate Measurement | B1033 | Trainer: pump/tank unit, paddle-wheel flow transmitter, rotameter (LPM/GPM), RTD temperature transmitter, 2 × DMM, hoses/banana leads | — |

Prep for the alt stream: book **B1033**; confirm every trainer bench has a
working power-supply module, pump/tank unit and the two DMMs; confirm **Siemens
TIA Portal** licences for the PLC lab; print each handout's instructor sign-off
sheet (4 sign-offs per lab).
